Number 15 is the seasons idea in one sentence.
Numbers 13 and 16 are toll booths on today's board.

chapters.title: When markets fall: buckets, collateral and rotation
chapters.kicker: A 20% crash does not hand 20% to someone else. But money really does slosh between buckets, and the timing of when you enter a bucket is most of the game.

blocks.text: Every big market drop brings the same post: the market lost a trillion dollars today, so someone on the other side must have made a trillion. It feels like conservation of money. If value left one place, it must have arrived somewhere. That intuition is mostly wrong, and understanding why it is wrong is one of the most useful things in this whole rulebook.
Market cap is a price tag, not a pile of cash

Market capitalization is a simple multiplication: the last price anyone traded at, times every share that exists. It is a valuation. It is not money sitting in a vault. When the price moves, the whole tag is rewritten, even though only a few shares actually changed hands.

blocks.caption: A company with 1,000 shares. Ten shares trade at a lower price and the value of all 1,000 shares is rewritten.

items: A company has 1,000 shares. The last trade was at $100, so its market cap is $100,000.
Bad news arrives. A nervous seller offers 10 shares and the best bid is $80. They trade.
The last price is now $80, so the market cap is now $80,000. Twenty thousand dollars of value is gone.
How much cash changed hands? Ten shares at $80, which is $800. The seller got $800 in cash. The buyer paid $800 in cash and got shares.
Nobody received the missing $20,000. It was never cash. It was an estimate of what all the shares were worth, and the estimate went down.

blocks.myth: When the stock market drops 20%, someone on the other side profited by that same 20%.
blocks.reality: Most of the drop is a repricing of paper value that nobody collects. Every share sold had a buyer who paid cash for it, so cash only changes hands, it does not appear from the crash. The people who do profit from a fall (short sellers, buyers of put options) win only what the other side of those specific contracts loses, which is a small slice of the headline number.

blocks.label: Picture this
blocks.text: Your street has 100 houses. One neighbor sells in a hurry for 20% below what similar houses fetched last month. An appraiser now marks every house on the street 20% lower. The street lost millions on paper in one afternoon, yet only one family actually sold, and one family actually bought. Nobody walked away with the millions. That is what a market crash headline is.
So does money just circulate? Not quite. It moves between buckets

The owner of this project put the next idea well: money is not a fixed pie that only circulates. It moves through different buckets, at different times, and each bucket sits on top of other buckets as collateral. That is right, with two refinements. First, the pie is not fixed: banks create money when they lend and it disappears when loans are repaid (chapter 6), so the total in the buckets can grow or shrink. Second, valuations move far more than money does, because a small flow of cash into a bucket can reprice everything already in it.

blocks.caption: Money rotates between buckets, and the buckets are stacked: one bucket's value is pledged to borrow money that fills the next.

items: Cash and bills: the safe bucket. It fills up when people are scared.
Bonds: fill up when people expect rates to fall or want steady income.
Stocks: fill up when people expect profits to grow.
Property: fills up when credit is cheap, because most of it is bought with loans.
Gold: fills up when people distrust the system or the currency.
Crypto and frontier assets: fill up last in a boom and empty first in a bust.

blocks.text: Collateral on top of collateral

Here is where the owner's phrase is exactly right. A bucket's value is often pledged to borrow money that fills another bucket. Stocks are pledged for a margin loan. Bonds are pledged in repo (a short loan backed by bonds) to buy more bonds. A house is pledged for a mortgage, and the bank pledges the mortgage to borrow from someone else. When prices rise, the collateral is worth more, so you can borrow more, so prices rise further. When prices fall, the same chain runs backwards: the lender asks for more collateral (a margin call), you must sell, the selling pushes prices lower, and the next borrower gets a margin call. That is why falls are often faster than rises.

The scary days in markets are rarely about people changing their minds. They are about collateral. In 2008 it was mortgage bonds pledged in repo. In 2022 British pension funds had to sell government bonds to meet margin calls on their hedges, which pushed bond prices down, which caused more margin calls, until the Bank of England stepped in. Watch who is forced to sell, not who wants to sell.
Early, late, and the price of being first

Because money rotates, timing matters. The first money into a bucket buys before the crowd, when the story is uncertain and the bucket might stay empty. It takes the most risk and, when it is right, earns the largest return, sometimes an outlier return. The last money in buys after prices have risen, when the story is obvious and everybody agrees. It takes a different risk: that it is buying from the early money on its way out. Neither is free money. The early buyer is paid for carrying uncertainty and being wrong often. The late buyer pays for comfort.

rows: Being wrong or too early, the bucket stays empty
Riding the repricing as others join
Mistaking a crowded trade for a safe one
Buying from early money that is leaving

blocks.text: What moves money between buckets

items: Interest rates and liquidity: when central banks make money cheap, it flows outward toward riskier buckets. When money gets dear, it flows back toward cash and bills.
Credit: lending creates new money that lands in some bucket first, usually property and financial assets (the Cantillon effect from chapter 16).
Supply and demand: new shares, new bonds and new coins dilute a bucket. Buybacks and scarcity concentrate it.
Fear and narrative: stories move flows faster than numbers do.
Rules: laws that force holders into a bucket (like stablecoin reserves that must hold Treasury bills) fill that bucket by design.
Rigging: it exists (insider trading, pump and dump schemes, spoofing) and is illegal in most markets, but most rotation is explained by the five forces above.

blocks.q: The stock market falls 20% and headlines say $10 trillion was wiped out. Where did the $10 trillion go?
blocks.a: Mostly nowhere. It was the paper value of all shares at the last traded price. The cash that changed hands in the selling went from buyers to sellers. Short sellers and put buyers gained only what their direct counterparties lost, a small fraction of the headline.

rules: A market cap is a price tag on the last trade, not cash. Crashes mostly erase paper value that nobody collects.
Money does not just circulate. It rotates between buckets, and buckets are pledged as collateral for each other.
Falls are faster than rises because collateral chains force selling.
Early money is paid for uncertainty, late money pays for comfort. Know which one you are.

connects.how: Why the pie is not fixed: loans create money and repayments destroy it.
Seasons of money decide which buckets fill and which drain.
The Cantillon effect explains which bucket new money reaches first.

chapters.title: Nation Inc.: taxes, interest and the hubs
chapters.kicker: Is tax a scam? Why did the Torah and the Quran forbid interest? Is a tax-free hub like the UAE cheating? Read the world's countries as companies competing on one leaderboard and the answers fall into place.

blocks.label: In 60 seconds
items: Each country works like a company: a finance department, a currency desk, billing, legal, security, sales and HR.

Tax is the subscription fee for the board itself: the money, the courts that protect your title and the security around them. It is not a scam, but who pays it and how well it is spent are fair fights.
Old religious bans on interest were early tools to stop debt from turning into permanent ownership. Islamic finance today still runs inside a dollar system built on interest.
Tax-free hubs like the UAE compete for people and capital that other countries paid to raise. It is legal and deliberate, and it is the leaderboard at work.

blocks.text: Read every country as a company

The fastest way through the jargon is to stop picturing countries as flags and start picturing them as companies. There are about 195 of them. Each has departments, staff, customers, a balance sheet, a credit rating and rivals. The leaderboard from chapter 11 is the ranking of these companies.

blocks.caption: A country drawn as a company. The names change from place to place. The jobs do not.

rows: Its credit rating and bond yields
Its currency's share of world reserves
Taxes on work carry about 86% of US federal receipts
Rule of law and kept promises
The pillars of a deep market in chapter 11
Who moves in and who moves out
About 60% of the Malaysian diaspora lives in Singapore

blocks.text: Is tax a scam?

A popular argument says tax is theft, or a scam that takes from workers and hands to elites. Go back to the board game from chapter 14. The game has been running for thousands of years, and it only works because someone keeps the board, issues the money, records who owns which square and stops players from simply seizing each other's property. That someone is the state, and the subscription fee is tax. Without it there is no common money, no court to defend your title deed, no land registry, no police and no army. You would be left trading by barter, and anyone stronger could take your land.

Tax also gives the money its value. Adam Smith noticed in 1776 that a ruler who demands taxes in a certain paper money gives that paper value. The German economist Georg Friedrich Knapp built a whole theory on the idea in 1905. Every American must pay federal tax in dollars, so every American needs dollars. That steady demand is one reason the dollar is accepted everywhere, long before anyone thinks about gold or oil.

The critics are not wrong about everything. Who pays matters. In the US, taxes on income and payroll carry about 86% of federal receipts, while gains on assets are taxed only when sold and can escape tax when passed on at death. Inflation is a tax nobody votes on. Spending can be wasteful or captured by insiders. So the honest verdict is: tax is not a scam. It is a fee. The real fights are over how big the fee is, who pays it, and whether the company spends it well.

blocks.myth: Tax is a scam. Without the state I would keep everything I earn.
blocks.reality: Without the state there is no money to earn in, no court to enforce your pay and no title to your home. The fair question is not whether to pay the fee, but whether it is set and spent fairly.

blocks.text: Why the holy books forbade interest

The Torah forbids lending at interest to a fellow member of the community (Exodus 22:25, Leviticus 25:36 to 37), while Deuteronomy 23:19 to 20 allows it with a foreigner. The Quran forbids riba and warns those who take it (Al-Baqarah 2:275 to 279). Medieval Christianity banned usury for centuries as well. Three traditions, far apart, reached the same rule. Why?

Because in an ancient farming world, interest on debt could grow faster than any harvest. A bad year forced a family to borrow, the interest compounded, and soon the family handed over its land, then its labor, sometimes its children. Debt turned into permanent ownership by the lender. The same book of Leviticus prescribed a Jubilee every fiftieth year, when land returned to its original families. Mesopotamian kings regularly declared clean slates that cancelled farmers' debts. These were resets built into the rules, so the board could never become permanently titled to a few. It is the same pressure chapter 19 describes today.

blocks.label: Picture this
blocks.text: Imagine Monopoly with one extra rule: every fifty laps, every street returns to the family that first held it, and all loans are torn up. Nobody can win forever, and nobody is a tenant forever. That was the Jubilee.

Islamic finance today, estimated at about $5 trillion to $6.5 trillion of assets in 2025 depending on who counts, replaces interest with sharing and trading. Instead of lending at interest, a bank can share the profits and losses of a venture, buy a house and sell it to you at a fixed markup paid in installments, or lease it to you. Islamic bonds, called sukuk, pay returns tied to real assets.

Two catches. First, many products end up paying something very close to interest in a different wrapper. In November 2007 the leading scholar Muhammad Taqi Usmani said that about 85% of sukuk did not comply with Islamic law because of buyback promises that guaranteed the money back, and the standards body AAOIFI tightened its rules in 2008. Second, the Gulf currencies are pegged to the dollar, so their interest rates follow the Federal Reserve. Interest-free finance still lives inside a dollar system that runs on interest.
The UAE: no income tax. Cheat, or strategy?

The UAE charges no personal income tax. It added a 5% VAT in 2018, a 9% corporate tax from June 2023 on profits above AED 375,000, and a 15% minimum tax on large multinationals from 2025. Much of the state's income comes from oil and gas, state companies and fees, and its sovereign funds are among the largest in the world. Its dirham is pegged to the dollar.

The result is a magnet. Henley and Partners estimated that about 9,800 millionaires would move to the UAE in 2025, more than to any other country. In company terms, the UAE hires experienced staff whose schooling, health care and early careers were paid for by other countries' taxpayers, at the moment those people earn the most. The home country trained them. The hub collects their best years and their capital.

blocks.label: The decode verdict
blocks.text: Cheating: no. It is legal and openly announced. A deliberate strategy to attract wealth built elsewhere: D1, decoded-strong, about 85%. Lucrative: yes, as long as oil income funds the state, the dollar peg holds and the region stays safe. Singapore, Switzerland, Monaco, Ireland for companies, and others play versions of the same game. The OECD's 15% global minimum tax, agreed by more than 130 countries in 2021, was the big countries' attempt to limit it.

The leaderboard leader plays by different rules. The United States is the only major country that taxes its citizens' full income wherever they live. Eritrea, the other usual example, charges its citizens abroad a flat 2%. An American who moves to Dubai still files a US tax return, and leaving for good means giving up citizenship and possibly paying an exit tax. Since 2010 a law called FATCA has made banks around the world report Americans' accounts. Only the company that owns the world's main currency and its payment pipes can keep its staff on the payroll after they leave.
Why this usually takes years to see

Taxes, interest, pegs, hubs, ratings and reserves are usually taught in different courses, each with its own jargon and messy charts, and rarely with the history and geopolitics that explain why they exist. That is why understanding money usually takes years of relooping. Read the countries as companies on one leaderboard, and the pieces snap into one picture: who issues the money, who pays the fee, who trains the talent, who collects it, and who sets the rules.

blocks.q: Why does a country that charges no income tax still need a state, a currency and courts?
blocks.a: Because the board still needs a keeper. The UAE funds its state mainly from oil, state companies and fees instead of income tax, but it still issues the dirham, runs courts and registries and provides security. The fee is collected another way.

blocks.q: Why did ancient rules ban interest or cancel debts?
blocks.a: Because compounding interest in a farming world turned bad harvests into lost land and lost freedom. Bans and jubilees stopped debt from turning into permanent ownership by lenders.

rules: Tax is the subscription fee for the board. Argue about its size, who pays and how it is spent, not whether it should exist.
Read a country like a company: its departments, its staff, its customers and its rivals for talent.
Interest bans and debt jubilees were ancient tools to stop debt from turning into permanent ownership.
Hubs grow by hiring talent and capital that other countries paid to raise.

chapters.title: The titled world: why abundance runs on credit, and who keeps the balance
chapters.kicker: Divide the world's wealth by everyone and it looks like plenty. Here is why most of that plenty is a price set on future credit, why the base layer was titled long ago, and what role each big country plays in keeping a crowded system from tipping over.

blocks.text: This is the last chapter before the Rulebook, and it pulls the whole book together around one thought experiment. Take everything the world owns, divide it by everyone alive, and ask: if there is so much, why do so many people feel they are locked out?
The thought experiment: divide it all

UBS estimates the world's personal wealth at about $470 trillion at the end of 2024. Divided by about 8.2 billion people, that is roughly $57,000 for every man, woman and child, or about $230,000 for a family of four. On paper the world is rich. Yet the same report finds that about 42% of adults own less than $10,000, while about 1.5% own more than $1 million.

blocks.caption: The equal share on paper against what adults actually hold. Brackets from the UBS Global Wealth Report 2025, end of 2024.

blocks.text: Now divide the base layer instead
The $57,000 is a nominal number. It is a price, measured in dollars at today's interest rates, not a quantity of things. To see the real pie, divide the base layer instead.

blocks.caption: Each person's equal share of the world, first in paper, then in real things. Cropland from FAO (2023), energy from the Energy Institute (2025).

blocks.text: Each person's share of the world's cropland is about 0.2 hectares, roughly a quarter of a football pitch, to grow all of their food. Their share of all the energy humanity used in 2025, about 600 exajoules, is about 20,000 kWh a year, the same as 23 old 100-watt bulbs burning day and night, to run every farm, factory, truck, home and data center on their behalf. Savills' value for all the world's farmland works out to about $5,800 a person. Measured in things, the world is far less abundant than $57,000 suggests. Measured in claims, it looks rich, because claims can multiply faster than farmland or power plants.

This is why the price of the base layer tends to climb in a credit-driven world. Each new round of credit creates more claims chasing the same farmland, the same city plots and the same energy. The claims multiply and the base layer does not, so its price rises. Owners of the base layer get richer without making anything new.
Why the pie is smaller than it looks

items: Most wealth is a price, not a pile. About two thirds of the world's net worth is real estate, and Savills values all the world's property at about $393 trillion at the start of 2025. Those values come from the last sales, as chapter 17 showed with market caps. If everyone tried to sell at once to share out the money, the price would collapse.

Prices are future income divided by the interest rate. When rates fell from the early 1980s to 2021, the same buildings and companies became worth far more without producing more. McKinsey found that global net worth rose from about $156 trillion in 2000 to about $514 trillion in 2020, while for every $1 of new investment, liabilities grew almost $4, about $2 of it debt. Most of the new wealth was revaluation, not new things.

Every financial asset is someone else's debt or someone's future income. Global debt reached about $365 trillion in mid-2026, about 310% of world output, according to the Institute of International Finance. A bond, a deposit or a loan is a claim on a borrower's future earnings. Count the claim as wealth and you must also count the debt.

What can really be shared each year is output, not prices. The world produces roughly $115 to $120 trillion of goods and services a year, about $14,000 per person, and most of that already pays for wages, rents, interest and taxes.

blocks.caption: A wide stack of claims balanced on a narrow base of real things. The higher the layer, the more it depends on future credit.

blocks.text: So the abundance we see is partly real, in machines, knowledge, networks and food, and partly a bet on future production, financed by credit and priced at today's interest rates. That is the owner's insight in plain terms: much of the world's apparent abundance is priced on future credit. When rates rise, as they did in 2026, the bet is repriced and the paper abundance shrinks, even though not one building or factory disappears.
Money is debt, and debt is money

There is a deeper reason the paper pie and the real pie differ. Almost all modern money is somebody's debt. Chapter 6 showed that a bank loan creates a deposit. Your bank balance is the bank's debt to you. A dollar bill is a liability of the Federal Reserve, which holds mostly government bonds against it, and those bonds are the government's debt, to be paid from future taxes. Money is debt, and debt is money. If every loan in the world were repaid tomorrow, most of the money would vanish with them.

blocks.caption: Every dollar someone owns is matched by a debt someone else owes. Only real things, gold and Bitcoin sit outside the mirror.

items: To grow the money supply, the system must grow debt. That is why total wealth and total debt keep rising together.
Paying debt down shrinks money. When too many people do it at once, as in 1929 to 1933, money disappears and prices fall.

Add up the whole world and every financial asset cancels out against someone's debt. What remains, the world's true net worth, is the value of its real things: land, buildings, machines and the rest of the base layer.
The exceptions are things that are nobody's IOU: gold, Bitcoin, land and goods. That is exactly why people run to them when they start to doubt the debts.

blocks.text: So the $57,000 is not $57,000 of stuff. Much of it is deposits, bonds and pension claims, each matched by a debt somewhere else, owed by a company, a bank or a government that must pay it from future income. Net out the IOUs and what is left is the base layer plus the machines and buildings on top, priced at whatever today's interest rates allow.
A world already titled

Underneath the claims sits the base layer: land, water, minerals, energy, ports, sea lanes, the best city plots, radio spectrum. Almost all of it was claimed long ago, recorded in a title registry or held by a state. Chapter 14 asked how a new player gets onto a board where no one gives out starting money. The harder truth is that the squares are already owned. Newcomers do not arrive on an empty board. They arrive as tenants.

When the base layer was up for grabs, it was often fought over with armies. European powers divided Africa among themselves after the Berlin Conference of 1884 to 1885. Japan pushed into Southeast Asia in 1941 after the United States cut off its oil. Iraq invaded oil-rich Kuwait in 1990. Today the contest is mostly fought with money instead: tariffs, sanctions, export controls on chips and rare earths, and who gets to price oil, finance mines and hold the world's savings. The wars over title turned into wars over price and access, though the older kind has not disappeared.
The generational seat at the table

Within countries, the same pattern runs between generations. In the United States, households headed by baby boomers, born from 1946 to 1964, hold about 52% of household net worth in mid-2026, while millennials and Gen Z together hold about 11%, according to analyses of the Federal Reserve's distributional accounts. Households headed by someone under 40 held about 6.6% in early 2026, down from about 12% in 1989. Older people always own more than younger ones, but the gap has widened, because the assets the older generation bought were revalued upward by falling rates, and the young must buy the same assets at the higher price, usually with credit.

blocks.label: Picture this
blocks.text: A Monopoly game where the first players bought every street while it was cheap. Late players start with only cash and pay rent on every lap. The bank keeps lending the late players money so the game can go on, because a game in which nobody can pay rent ends for the owners too.

That last line is the key to the whole system. Owners need newcomers. Rents, mortgages, share prices and pension promises only hold if new buyers and tenants keep paying. So the system cannot lock newcomers out completely. It lets them in through wages, credit and a little inflation, on terms that keep the owners' titles valuable. This is the quiet balance the money managers of the world are actually running.
Four levers that keep the balance

items: Credit: lend newcomers the price of a seat. It keeps asset prices up and lets the young buy in, at the cost of decades of payments to lenders.
Inflation: quietly shifts value from savers and lenders to borrowers, who are often younger. It shrinks old debts and lifts wages in money terms. Chapter 9 showed why indebted systems choose it.

Taxes and transfers: pensions, health care, child accounts and income support move part of the owners' income to people without assets. Chapter 14 and the Desk looked at what a universal income can and cannot carry.
New frontiers: new industries create new things to own before they are titled. Railways, oil, the internet and now AI, compute, energy and space are where newcomers can get title early.

blocks.text: When all four levers fail at once, history offers darker resets. The historian Walter Scheidel argued in The Great Leveler (2017) that across recorded history only four forces have reliably shrunk inequality on a large scale: mass-mobilization war, transformative revolution, state collapse and deadly pandemics. The levers above exist, in large part, to keep those four away.
Who plays which role

blocks.caption: A simplified map of the roles. Real countries mix several roles, and roles change over time.

rows: Issues the reserve currency, borrows and buys from the world, guarantees security
Debt, hollowed industry, division at home
The world's workshop and a giant saver, now the main rival in hardware
Dependence on foreign buyers, low household spending
High-tech exporters that lend their surpluses back
Weak home demand, exposure to US policy
Gulf states and other energy exporters
Supply the base-layer fuel and recycle surpluses through state funds
Oil price swings, dependence on protection
Resource exporters such as Australia, Brazil, Canada, Indonesia and Africa's miners
Price swings and fights over title
Hubs: UK, Switzerland, Singapore, Hong Kong, UAE
Custodians, bankers, courts and meeting places
India and other large, young economies
Entering on terms set by others
Referees and lenders of last resort
Questions about whose rules they enforce

blocks.text: Each role balances the others. Exporters need the US to keep buying. The US needs them to keep lending. Energy and resource exporters need both. Hubs need everyone to keep trusting the pipes. Countries also change roles: Britain went from workshop to banker, and China from workshop to rival. Every role change is a moment of stress for the whole system, which is why this desk watches the China truce, the Gulf and Japan so closely.
Sovereign wealth funds: the countries' investment arms

Chapter 18 drew every country as a company with an investment arm. That arm is the sovereign wealth fund: a state-owned fund that turns a country's surplus, usually from oil, gas or trade, into ownership of assets around the world. Global SWF counted sovereign funds holding more than $15 trillion at the end of 2025. There are well over a hundred of them, but about a dozen giants hold most of the money, so twelve is a good number to remember.

blocks.caption: The five jobs a sovereign fund can do. Most big funds do two or three at once.

rows: Saver. Owns about 1.5% of all listed companies
Saver. Roots in 1953, the oldest of its kind
Developer and strategic arm: new cities, sports, games
Saver and strategic arm, trophy assets abroad
Stabilizer behind the Hong Kong dollar peg
Holding company for the airline, banks and property

blocks.text: Sizes are approximate. Norway publishes its value every quarter, but several giants, including ADIA, GIC and China's SAFE, publish no official figure, so trackers estimate them and do not always agree. The UAE alone runs four funds above $250 billion: ADIA, Investment Corporation of Dubai, Mubadala and ADQ.

items: Stabilizer: a shock absorber that saves in boom years and spends when oil or export prices crash.
Saver: turns a resource that will run out into a permanent stake in the world's companies, for generations not yet born.
Reserve investor: earns more on a country's surplus dollars than Treasury bills would.
Developer: builds new industries at home so the country is not stuck selling one raw material. Malaysia's Khazanah Nasional plays this role.
Strategic arm: buys stakes, ports, chip plants, football clubs and game studios abroad, which bring influence and access as well as returns.

blocks.text: Read these funds through this chapter's lens. They convert a base layer that will run out, oil and gas, into titles on the rest of the world: shares, buildings, ports and companies. Norway turned its oil into about 1.5% of every listed company on earth. A small country cannot hold the deep-market crown, but it can buy a slice of the board itself. It is also how much of the petrodollar from chapter 5 comes back to the US and Europe, not only into Treasuries but into their companies.

The fund idea also touches the universal income debate. Alaska's Permanent Fund, built from oil revenue and worth about $89 billion, pays every eligible resident a yearly dividend: $1,200 in 2026, made up of $1,000 plus a $200 energy relief payment. It is the closest thing in the United States to a citizen's share of a titled base layer. The United States has historically had no national fund of this kind. A February 2025 executive order asked for a plan for one, and whether it becomes real is a tell worth watching.

blocks.q: Why would an oil country rather own a slice of the world's companies than spend all its oil money at home?
blocks.a: Because oil runs out and its price swings. Spreading the money across the world's companies turns a temporary resource into permanent, diversified income, and avoids flooding the home economy with cash it cannot absorb, which would cause Dutch disease.

blocks.text: Decoding the balance: a plan, or incentives?

blocks.label: The decode verdict
blocks.text: A secret global plan by money managers to keep newcomers out forever: D3, folklore, about 10% as stated. Policy that consistently protects asset prices, because owners vote, lend, fund campaigns and hold the pension savings: D1, decoded-strong, about 80%. After 2008 and again in 2020 central banks moved quickly to support asset prices. Nobody needs to coordinate. Each actor's incentive points the same way: keep the titles valuable, keep the newcomers paying, and keep the four horsemen away.

This is why the future this desk studies matters so much. Robots, AI and cheap energy could enlarge the base layer itself. If newcomers can own a share of that new capacity before it is titled, the gap can close. If the same owners title it first, the gap widens. Who gets title to the new base layer of energy, compute, data and orbit is the ownership question of this generation.
The whole book in one chain

items: Money is a trusted promise (chapter 1). Its anchor moved from metal to the dollar to government bonds (chapters 2 to 6 and Level 2 chapter 1).
Banks create most money as loans, so the system needs ever more credit (chapter 6 and Level 2 chapter 2).
The seasons decide who wins, borrowers or savers, and debt decides which season governments choose (chapters 7 and 8).
Nations compete for the deep-market crown, and smaller currencies live by its rules (chapters 11 and 12).
The ruler we measure with keeps shrinking (chapter 13).
Newcomers start on a board with no free money, and new rails are laid on old anchors (chapters 14 and 15).
Paper values are claims on the future and can fall fast (chapters 16 and 17).
Every country runs like a company on that leaderboard, with taxes as its subscription fee and hubs competing for its talent (chapter 18).
Underneath it all, money is debt, the abundance on paper rests on credit, and the base layer was titled long ago. The system's real job is balancing owners and newcomers without calling the horsemen.

blocks.myth: If the world's wealth were shared out, everyone would be comfortable.
blocks.reality: Only on paper. Most of that wealth is the price of homes and companies at today's interest rates. Sell it all to divide it and the price collapses. What could really be shared is each year's output, about $14,000 per person, and most of it already pays for wages, rents, interest and taxes.

blocks.q: Global personal wealth is about $470 trillion. Why can't it simply be handed out as $57,000 to each person?
blocks.a: Because most of it is the price of existing assets, valued at the last trade and at today's interest rates, and much of it is matched by debts. Selling it all to share it out would crash the price. What is really available each year is output, about $14,000 per person.

blocks.q: Why does a system that favors owners still lend money to newcomers?
blocks.a: Because owners need newcomers to keep paying rent, interest and share prices. If newcomers could pay nothing, the owners' titles would lose their value. Credit keeps the game going.

rules: Wealth on paper is a price, not a pile.
Every financial asset is someone's debt or someone's future income.
The base layer was titled long ago. Newcomers enter through wages, credit and new frontiers.
Look for the next base layer before it is titled.
When a base layer runs out, the winners are those who turned it into titles first.

Why paper values vanish when everyone sells at once.
Where new money lands first, between countries.
Why indebted systems choose inflation over deflation.

chapters.title: Crypto: Set 2 money, dissected
chapters.kicker: Bitcoin, stablecoins and twenty million other tokens, sorted into three families, tested against the jobs of money, and taken apart with six questions you can use on any coin you ever hear about.

blocks.label: In 60 seconds
items: Chapter 1 said money is a trusted record of who can claim what. Crypto is a new way to keep that record: a shared ledger that no single bank or government runs.

There are three very different families. Bitcoin is a scarce asset that is nobody's debt. Stablecoins are digital dollars backed by Treasury bills. Everything else is closer to a share in a platform, a loyalty point or a lottery ticket.
Lumping them together as 'crypto' is the most common mistake. Each family answers the money questions differently.
So far Set 2 is not replacing Set 1. Stablecoins carry dollars onto new rails, and Bitcoin competes with gold as a neutral store. Set 1 is absorbing Set 2.
To judge any token, ask six questions: who issues it, whose debt is it, what anchors it, which job of money does it do, who can freeze it, and where does its return come from.

items.d: A record of who owns what. Every money in history has been one.
A ledger copied across thousands of computers, updated in blocks and very hard to change afterward.
A unit recorded on a blockchain. It can stand for a coin, a dollar, a share or a vote.
The secret password that moves your tokens. Lose it and nobody can restore it.
A token built to stay worth $1, usually backed by dollars and Treasury bills.

blocks.text: Why crypto matters for what money is

Go back to chapter 1. Money is not the paper or the metal. It is a trusted record of who can claim what, and the fight has always been over who keeps the record: the temple, the king, the goldsmith, the central bank, the commercial bank. Crypto's real invention, published in 2008, is a record kept by a network instead of a keeper. The rules are written in code, anyone can check the ledger, and no single party can quietly edit it.

blocks.label: Picture this
blocks.text: On 3 January 2009 the first Bitcoin block was created with a newspaper headline written into it: 'Chancellor on brink of second bailout for banks', from The Times of London. Whoever built it was making a point in the middle of the financial crisis: here is a money whose ledger no bank can lose and no government can inflate. The creator, known only as Satoshi Nakamoto, has never been identified.

That is why crypto belongs in this book. It is the first serious attempt since gold to create money that is nobody's debt and nobody's ledger. Chapter 19 showed that almost all modern money is someone's IOU. Bitcoin is the deliberate exception. Whether or not it succeeds, it forces every government to answer an old question in a new form: who should keep the record?
Set 1 and Set 2

This project splits the money world into two sets. Set 1 is the old anchors: gold, government bonds and bank credit. Set 2 is the new rails: blockchains, stablecoins and tokens. After three research rounds the desk's finding is that Set 1 is absorbing Set 2, an acquisition rather than a merger. Stablecoins must hold Treasury bills by law, Wall Street sells Bitcoin through exchange-traded funds approved in January 2024, and asset managers are moving Treasury funds onto blockchains.

blocks.caption: Each new rail ends up tied back to an old anchor.

blocks.text: The three families

blocks.caption: Three families that share a technology and little else. Sizes from mid-October 2026.

blocks.text: Family 1: Bitcoin, digital gold

items: Fixed supply: the code caps it at 21 million coins. About 20.08 million had been mined by August 2026, and an estimated 10% to 20% of those are lost forever with forgotten keys.
Slowing issuance: new coins are created as a reward for running the network, and the reward halves about every four years. The last halving, in April 2024, cut it to 3.125 coins per block.
Nobody's debt: there is no issuer to redeem it and no one who owes you anything. On chapter 19's mirror it sits beside gold.
Size: about $80,900 a coin and about $1.63 trillion in total on 15 October 2026, roughly 60% of all crypto by value.
Wild swings: it fell about 77% from its November 2021 peak to November 2022, and has had several falls of that size.

Governments are circling: a March 2025 executive order created a US Strategic Bitcoin Reserve from coins already seized in court cases. The Treasury Secretary said in August 2025 the US would not buy more.

blocks.text: Test it against the three jobs of money. As a store of value it is a real candidate, scarce and owed by no one, but its swings are far too large for most people's savings. As a medium of exchange it is rarely used, because, as chapter 9 showed with the 10,000-bitcoin pizza, people spend the money that melts and keep the one they expect to grow. As a unit of account it barely exists: almost nothing is priced in Bitcoin. Its realistic job is a neutral store of value next to gold.
Family 2: Stablecoins, dollars on new rails

A stablecoin is a token that tries to stay worth exactly $1. A company holds dollars and short-term Treasury bills, issues a token for each dollar deposited and destroys it when the dollar is taken back out. In October 2026 stablecoins totaled about $303.8 billion, led by Tether's USDT and Circle's USDC. Under the GENIUS Act, signed in July 2025 and taking full effect on 18 January 2027, compliant issuers must hold reserves in cash and Treasury bills of 93 days or less, and may not pay holders interest. The issuer keeps the interest on the bills.

Stablecoins are Set 1 wearing Set 2 clothes. They carry the dollar to anyone with a phone, including savers in weak-currency countries like those in chapter 12, and every new stablecoin dollar is a new buyer of US Treasury bills. Stablecoins already hold about 4.27% of all T-bills. That is why Washington legalized private stablecoins while a January 2025 executive order blocked work on a Federal Reserve digital dollar for the public. A stablecoin is a dollar IOU, so on chapter 19's mirror it sits on the debt side.

Stable does not mean safe. In March 2023 USDC briefly fell to about 87 cents when $3.3 billion of its reserves were stuck at the failing Silicon Valley Bank. In May 2022 TerraUSD, a so-called algorithmic stablecoin backed mainly by its own sister token instead of dollars, collapsed from about $40 billion to almost nothing within days.
Family 3: everything else

More than 20 million tokens had been created by 2025, most through do-it-yourself launch sites, and CoinGecko counts more than half of the ones it tracks as already dead. The survivors follow a handful of business models.

rows: Fuel to run apps on a blockchain, such as Ether (about $288B in October 2026)
Collect fees from everyone who uses the network
A share in a toll road
Loyalty points, or shares without shareholder rights
Votes over how a protocol is run
Bonds, funds or property recorded on a blockchain, such as BlackRock's BUIDL
The same asset with a new ledger

blocks.text: Tokenized US Treasury funds grew about fiftyfold from early 2024 to about $16 billion by August 2026, which is the clearest sign of Set 1 moving onto Set 2 rails. Most of the rest are not money at all in the sense of chapter 1. They are claims on a business, a network or a hope.

blocks.label: Not crypto, but a cousin
blocks.text: A central bank digital currency uses some of the same technology for the opposite purpose: the state keeps the ledger and can see every payment. China's e-CNY is the largest. Since January 2026 its wallet balances count as deposits at commercial banks and can earn interest. Bitcoin was built to take the ledger away from the state. A central bank digital currency brings it closer.
How to dissect any token: six questions

blocks.caption: Six questions that work on any coin, old or new. The last one catches most scams.

items: Who issues it, and can they make more? Find the supply rule and who is able to change it.
Whose debt is it? If someone must redeem it, it is an IOU and you are trusting them. If no one owes it, its value rests only on demand.
What anchors its value? Reserves, scarcity, fees from a working network, or nothing but attention.
Which job of money does it do: spend, store or measure? Or is it really a share, a coupon or a lottery ticket?
Who runs the ledger, and who can freeze or change it? An issuer that can freeze your coins is a bank in all but name.
Where does the return come from? If it pays a yield, someone must be paying it. If you cannot name who, the yield may be paid with newer investors' money.

blocks.caption: Try it. Pick a token and read its dissection. Compare Bitcoin with a stablecoin, then with a meme coin.

blocks.text: Question six would have saved a lot of people in 2022. Terra's Anchor platform paid about 20% a year on its stablecoin when most dollar savings paid under 2%, and at its peak held about $14 billion. The return was topped up from reserves rather than earned, so when the reserves ran low the whole structure collapsed. The same question applied to the FTX exchange, which collapsed in November 2022 after customer deposits were moved to its sister trading firm.
Where crypto sits on the layers of money

blocks.caption: Bitcoin sits beside gold at the narrow, solid bottom because it is nobody's debt. Stablecoins sit on top of Treasuries. Most other tokens belong with the riskiest claims near the top.

blocks.myth: Crypto is backed by nothing, so it is all worthless.
blocks.reality: Some tokens are backed by nothing and are worth nothing. Stablecoins are backed by dollars and bills. Bitcoin is backed by nothing in the way gold is backed by nothing: its value rests on scarcity and demand. Judge each one with the six questions, not by the label.

blocks.myth: Bitcoin will replace the dollar.
blocks.reality: Not as things stand. Almost nothing is priced in Bitcoin, few people spend it, and its swings are too large for wages and rent. Its realistic job is a neutral store of value next to gold. The challenger on the spending side is the stablecoin, and that is the dollar itself.

blocks.text: Why it matters for the future this desk studies

items: It tests who keeps the record. Every government now has to choose between private stablecoins, a state digital currency, or leaving the old bank ledger alone.
It extends the dollar. Stablecoins are becoming one of the largest new sources of demand for US Treasury bills, the captive demand Level 2 chapter 1 described.

It offers a neutral store. If trust in all government debts weakens, Bitcoin and gold are the two assets that are nobody's IOU. The desk's scenario of a neutral reserve layer stands at about 15% to 2028, 23% from 2028 to 2035 and 28% from 2035 to 2050.
It moves the ledger itself. Tokenized Treasuries and funds could make settlement instant, which changes who earns the float, the fees and the data.

blocks.text: The owner's question: what if the dollar ruler disappears?

blocks.label: The owner's question
blocks.text: Today everything, a share, a company bond, a token, has an easy measuring stick, because the dollar is there. Remove that layer, and we would probably learn to price things in Bitcoin. But right now crypto keeps getting absorbed into Set 1, because most of the world still settles in currencies. If tokens get good enough that nobody needs to convert Solana into stablecoins to buy things, and so many tokens can exist, where does their value come from? It still seems to come from base-layer credit and bond money. And if anyone lucky enough, a lottery winner or someone with a big enough yield, can launch their own token, it looks like a utopia. The opportunity seems enormous, and this is where it stops making sense.

This is chapter 1's question in its newest form: what makes something money, and who decides how everything is measured? It untangles in five pieces, followed by the questions worth carrying with you.
1. The ruler is the hardest job of money

Money has three jobs: spend, store and measure. Crypto has made real progress on the first two. The third, being the ruler everything is priced in, is the hardest, and no token has won it. When you pay with a token through a crypto debit card, the shop's price was set in dollars and your token was sold for dollars at the till. The conversion is invisible, not absent. The European Central Bank finds crypto and stablecoins below 1% of in-store payments in the euro area, in both 2024 and 2026.

blocks.caption: Why the dollar keeps the ruler: every link in an ordinary life is a dollar contract.

blocks.text: The ruler belongs to whatever debts and taxes are written in. Your salary, your rent, your landlord's mortgage, the bank's loans, the government's bonds and your taxes are all dollar contracts. A token can become the ruler only when those debts start being written in it. Chapter 18 showed that taxes give a money its value. El Salvador tested the opposite. It made Bitcoin legal tender in 2021, but its debts, wages and taxes stayed in dollars, use stayed low, and in January 2025, as part of a $1.4 billion IMF deal, it made accepting Bitcoin optional and dropped the state's promise to convert it to dollars.
2. Many monies, one ruler: why markets always rebuild a hub

blocks.caption: Six monies with no common ruler need 15 exchange rates. With one ruler in the middle, each needs only one price.

blocks.text: If every token traded directly against every other, each pair would need its own price. With 10 monies that is 45 exchange rates. With 1,000 it is 499,500. With the more than 20 million tokens created by 2025 it would be about 200 trillion. Nobody can think in that many prices, so markets always choose one hub that everything else is priced through. That is how barter turned into money in chapter 1, and it is happening again inside crypto, where most trading runs through a dollar stablecoin, Ether or Bitcoin acting as the hub.

blocks.caption: Try it. Slide from 2 monies to 20 million and watch how many exchange rates you would need without a common ruler.

blocks.label: This happened before
blocks.text: From 1837 to 1863 America had no national paper currency. Hundreds of banks printed their own notes, and each note traded at its own discount depending on the bank's reputation and how far away it was. Shopkeepers kept bank note reporters, booklets listing what each note was worth and which ones were forgeries. It was a world of many tokens. It ended when Congress taxed state bank notes at 10% in 1865, and their circulation fell from $143 million to $4 million within two years. The ruler went back to one national dollar.

The economist Friedrich Hayek argued in 1976, in The Denationalisation of Money, that private monies should compete and the public would choose the most stable one. Crypto is the first large-scale test of his idea. So far the public keeps choosing the most stable token on offer, and that token is a dollar.
3. Where a token's value really comes from

Your instinct is half right. Today almost every token's price is a dollar price, and most of the money that buys tokens was born as dollar credit, so crypto prices tend to rise when dollar credit is easy and fall when it tightens. But the deeper source of any money's value is the base layer from chapter 19: the real goods, work and assets people will hand over for it. A token is worth what someone will give up to hold it. If everyone held tokens and nobody produced anything, every token would buy nothing.

Bitcoin is scarce, but crypto is not. One coin can be capped at 21 million while anyone can launch a new one in minutes, and more than 20 million have been launched. Each new token is a new claim competing for the same real goods, the same attention and the same buyers' dollars. That is chapter 19's picture again: the claims multiply, and the base layer does not.
4. The lottery winner who launches a token

blocks.caption: The life of a typical launch. Bars show the price. The dashed arrow is where the dollars go.

blocks.text: Launching a token is printing money, and the profit has an old name: seigniorage, from chapter 16. A token costs almost nothing to create. When its founders sell part of it for dollars, they turn newly printed units into real buying power, exactly as a government does when it issues money. That buying power comes from the buyers. Unless the token's network produces something people pay for, the founders' gain is the later buyers' loss. That is why the utopia feels so big: the power to issue money has been opened to everyone, but the pool of real goods all those monies can buy has not grown with it.

rows: Runs a network people pay to use
Users pay fees for a real service, such as settlement or storage
Moves a real asset onto a faster ledger
Cheaper, quicker settlement saves real costs
Launches a token and sells it to later buyers
Seigniorage moves dollars from late buyers to early ones
Pays a high yield from new deposits
Returns come from newer money, as at Terra in 2022

blocks.text: 5. So where is the real opportunity?

items: New rails: cheaper, faster payments across borders, especially for people in weak-currency countries, mostly using dollar stablecoins.
Settlement: tokenized Treasuries and funds that settle in seconds, cutting into the float and fees banks earn today.
Money for machines: AI agents paying each other per request, which this project found already happens mostly in dollar tokens.
Early title to new networks: owning part of a network people truly pay to use, before it is titled. Chapter 19's rule applies: look for the next base layer before it is titled.

The ruler itself: if trust in all government debt ever broke, the next ruler would be whatever is hardest and most widely accepted. Gold did that job for thousands of years, Bitcoin is a candidate, and this project's founding question asks whether energy could be one. The desk puts an energy or compute standard at about 1% to 2028, 3% from 2028 to 2035 and 10% from 2035 to 2050.

blocks.text: The opportunity is real but narrower than it looks. Most of the lasting value is in building rails and owning networks that produce something. Much of the rest is seigniorage passing from late buyers to early ones.
Questions worth carrying with you

blocks.q: If your salary were paid in Solana, what would you pay your rent in, and what is your landlord's mortgage written in?
blocks.a: Dollars, and dollars. Every link in the chain is a dollar contract, so the token is converted somewhere even when you never see it. The ruler changes only when the debts change.

blocks.q: If Bitcoin became the ruler, what would happen to everyone with a mortgage?
blocks.a: If Bitcoin kept rising against goods, prices in Bitcoin would fall and debts written in Bitcoin would get heavier every year. Chapter 9's deflation debate applies: borrowers lose, savers win, and with no central bank there is no lender of last resort in a crisis.

blocks.q: Who would set interest rates in a world of a thousand tokens?
blocks.a: No one centrally. Each token's lenders and borrowers would set their own, and the most trusted token's rate would become the benchmark, the way the Treasury yield is today. The hub returns.

blocks.q: When AI agents pay each other, which ruler will they use?
blocks.a: So far the dollar, through stablecoins. Machines need stable prices even more than people do, because they price millions of tiny transactions. A machine economy is more likely to strengthen the dollar ruler than replace it, unless energy or compute itself becomes the unit.

blocks.q: If anyone can launch a token, what stops the world from drowning in money?
blocks.a: Nothing stops the launching. What stops the drowning is that buyers ignore most tokens, which is why more than half are already dead. Free issuance makes money cheap to create and trust expensive to earn.

blocks.text: General education, not advice. Crypto adds risks that bank money does not have: lost keys with no reset button, hacks, scams that target newcomers, exchanges that fail with customers' money inside, and rules that can change by executive order. Anyone who holds it should know which of the three families they own, and the answer to all six questions.

blocks.q: Is a dollar stablecoin closer to Bitcoin or to a bank deposit?
blocks.a: To a bank deposit. It is an IOU from an issuer, backed by dollars and Treasury bills, worth a dollar only as long as the issuer can redeem it. Bitcoin is nobody's IOU.

blocks.q: A new token promises 30% a year, paid in the token itself. Which of the six questions matters most?
blocks.a: Question six: where does the return come from? If the yield is paid in newly created tokens or from newer investors' money, the high number is a warning, not a feature.

blocks.q: Why do people spend dollars and stablecoins but hold Bitcoin?
blocks.a: Gresham's law from chapter 9: people spend the money they expect to lose value and keep the one they expect to gain.

rules: Crypto is three families, not one. Know which one you are looking at.
Ask whose debt it is. Bitcoin is nobody's IOU. A stablecoin is someone's IOU.
If you cannot say where a yield comes from, the yield is the product being sold.
Set 2 rails keep ending up tied to Set 1 anchors.
The ruler belongs to whatever debts and taxes are written in.
Bitcoin is scarce. Crypto is not.
Launching a token is printing money. Ask who pays for it.

chapters.title: The Rulebook
chapters.kicker: What each generation learned the hard way, written down so the next one does not have to.

blocks.text: Families pass down recipes, tools and stories. They rarely pass down money lessons, because money talk feels private or shameful, and because each generation's crisis feels unique while it is happening. So each generation relearns the same lessons at full price. This chapter is the remedy: a short rulebook, and a list of the mistakes behind it.
Those who cannot remember the past are condemned to repeat it.
blocks.by: George Santayana, The Life of Reason, 1905

blocks.text: How to use the rulebook

items: Read the rules once straight through. Most will now feel obvious, because the chapters built them.
Pick three rules that you are breaking today. Write them where you will see them.
Before any big money decision, such as a loan, a house, a business or an investment, scan the list and ask which rules apply.
Read the mistakes list with someone younger than you. Ask which mistake they think their own generation is making now.
Add your own rule when life teaches you one. A rulebook that stops growing stops being useful.

blocks.text: The shape of the rules

rows: Your understanding: see the promise behind the paper
Your savings: know what melts and what hardens
Your freedom: never become a forced seller
Your judgment: see who sets the rules and who earns the tolls
Your future: turn income into ownership

blocks.label: Picture this
blocks.text: Think of the rulebook as a ship's logbook kept across generations. Each captain wrote down the storms they met, the rocks they hit and the stars that guided them home. The next captain cannot avoid every storm. But a captain who has read the log will recognize the sky before the storm arrives.

The full rulebook and the generational mistakes follow this chapter. They are written to be copied, shared and argued with. They are general education about how money works, not financial advice for any particular person. Where a rule touches your own situation, test it against your own numbers, and against a second opinion.

blocks.q: Which rule from the whole guide would have saved the most people in 2008?
blocks.a: Several apply, but the strongest is: borrow only what you can service through a bad season without selling. Many households and banks were forced sellers when house prices fell.

blocks.q: Why does each generation repeat money mistakes?
blocks.a: Because the last crisis fades from memory, calm years breed confidence, and each new boom tells a story about why this time is different. Writing lessons down and passing them on is the cheapest defense.

rules: Write your lessons down and pass them on. Memory fades, logs do not.

chapters.title: Bonds: a ticket you can resell, and where it touches your life
chapters.kicker: A bond is a ticket you can resell: you pay RM100, it pays you RM4 a year, and you get RM100 back at the end. This chapter builds everything from that one ticket, then shows where bonds touch your own life, how to check your own exposure once a month, and how to weigh scary bond headlines before you feel them.

items: A bond is a ticket. You pay RM100. It pays you RM4 every year. At the end you get your RM100 back.
You can keep the ticket to the end, or resell it. Resale happens on the secondary market, through dealers.
When new tickets pay more, old tickets are worth less. Rates up, prices down. If you hold to the end, the dip disappears.
Bonds touch you even if you never buy one: your EPF, your bank, your loans, the ringgit, prices and taxes.
The same rise in rates hurts some people and helps others. A young saver with decades ahead mostly gains.
Check your own exposure once a month with six public dials and five questions, and weigh every scary headline on the SCALES.

blocks.label: How to learn this chapter
blocks.text: Read each part once. Then close the page and answer the stop-box questions from memory. Testing yourself beats rereading: in a classic study, students who tested themselves remembered 61% a week later, against 40% for those who reread (Roediger and Karpicke, 2006). Guess before you open each curiosity question. A wrong guess still helps you remember. And come back in a few days: spacing it out works better than one long read. You do not need a special learning style. Everyone learns better from words plus a picture.
This chapter comes in three parts of about ten minutes each. Each part ends with a stop box. Stop at any box and come back another day.
Part 1 of 3. The ticket and its second life
1. Should these three people worry?
Imagine tomorrow's headline: "Bond market crash". Meet three people. They are made up, but their situations are common.

items: Aisyah, 23, in Kuala Lumpur. First job, RM3,800 a month. About RM15,000 in EPF and RM5,000 in a fixed deposit. A fixed-rate car loan. She hopes to study abroad in three years.
The Rahman family in Penang. A floating home loan of RM400,000 over 35 years. About RM250,000 in EPF between them, and RM20,000 in a bond and sukuk fund.
Linda, 68, retired in the United States. $600,000 of savings: $240,000 in a bond fund, $300,000 in shares, $60,000 in Treasury bills.

blocks.text: Guess now: which of them should care about the headline? Keep your guess. By the end of the chapter you will be able to answer for each of them, and for yourself.
2. A bond is a ticket

Forget finance for a moment. The government sells you a ticket for RM100. The ticket says three things. It pays you RM4 every year. It ends on a fixed date, say in ten years. On that date the government buys it back from you for RM100.

blocks.caption: One ticket carries the whole chapter. You lend RM100, collect RM4 a year, and get RM100 back at the end.

blocks.text: That ticket is a bond. You lent the government RM100. The RM4 a year is your reward for waiting. A company can sell the same kind of ticket. So can a state, or a bank.

items.d: The ticket: a promise to pay you a fixed amount each year and your money back on a set date.
The amount paid back at the end. RM100 in our ticket.
The fixed yearly payment. RM4 in our ticket, or 4%.
The end date, when the ticket is bought back.
What the ticket really earns you per year at the price you pay today.

blocks.label: Malaysia note
blocks.text: About half of Malaysia's government paper is sukuk (GII). A sukuk gives you a share in an asset or its rent, not a loan. The ticket picture still works for price and resale. Only the word loan does not fit.
3. The seesaw: why your ticket's price moves

A month after you buy, the government sells new tickets that pay RM5 a year. Now try to resell yours. Nobody will pay RM100 for a ticket paying RM4 when a new one pays RM5. So your price drops until a buyer earns about the same as on a new ticket.

items: Worked example. Your ticket pays RM4, has 10 years left, and new tickets pay RM5. A buyer will pay about RM92.28. They get RM4 a year plus a RM7.72 gain at the end, which works out to about 5% a year.
Your turn, half done. New tickets pay RM3 instead. Is your RM4 ticket worth more or less than RM100? (It is worth more, about RM108.53, because it pays more than the new ones.)
Your turn. A ticket with only 2 years left, when new tickets pay RM5. Does it fall more or less than the 10-year ticket? (Much less, about 1.9%, because only two years of too little pay are left.)

blocks.caption: Rates and prices sit on a seesaw. When new tickets pay more, old tickets are worth less, and the other way round.
Try it. Three bonds, all bought for $1,000 and all paying $50 a year. Drag the rate new bonds pay and watch their prices. The black line is the $1,000 you paid.

blocks.text: Two rules fall out of the seesaw. Rates up, prices down. And the longer the ticket, the bigger the swing: a 30-year ticket falls about 15% when new tickets pay one point more, a 2-year ticket about 2%. These figures are a model worked out for this chapter.

blocks.myth: If a bond's price falls, the government must be in trouble.
blocks.reality: Usually it only means new tickets pay more. The government still owes you every RM4 and your RM100. The price matters only if you sell before the end.

items.q: You pay RM100 for a 10-year ticket paying RM4. Next month new tickets pay RM5. What can you sell yours for, and when does that loss stop mattering?
items.a: About RM92.28 (model). If you hold to the end, you still get every RM4 and your RM100 back, so the dip only matters if you sell early.

blocks.text: 4. The resale stall: the secondary market

There are two markets. The first sale happens at a ticket booth: the government's auction. Money goes to the government. Every sale after that happens at a resale stall, the secondary market. One investor sells to another, usually through a dealer. The government gets nothing from these resales. It still watches the price closely, because the resale price tells it what its next auction will cost.

blocks.caption: The booth sells new tickets. The resale stall is where old tickets change hands, and the dealer earns the gap between its two prices.

items: You want to sell. You contact a dealer, usually a bank's trading desk or a broker.
The dealer shows two prices. It buys at RM99.50 and sells at RM99.60. The gap is its fee for always being ready. On RM10,000 of tickets, buying and selling costs you about RM10.
Most bond trades happen between dealers and clients, not on a public screen like shares. You usually see a quote, not the whole market.
The buyer also pays you the interest you earned since the last coupon. Then the ticket and the cash swap accounts, normally within a day or two.

rows: about RM6.2 billion, up from RM3.8 billion in 2024

blocks.text: The gap between the two prices is the price of being able to leave. It is tiny in calm years. It jumps exactly when everyone wants out. In March 2020 even the safest US bonds were hard to sell, and the Fed bought $1.27 trillion of them in five weeks to calm the market.

items.q: Who owns most of Malaysia's government bonds, foreigners or Malaysians?
items.a: Malaysians. Residents held 78.5% at the end of 2025 and foreigners 21.5%. Pension funds such as EPF and the banks each hold roughly a third of the whole market (Bank Negara Bond Market Report 2025, worked out from its resident shares).

items.q: How much bigger is the US bond resale market than Malaysia's?
items.a: US Treasuries trade about $1.21 trillion a day. Malaysian government bonds trade about RM6.2 billion, roughly US$1.5 billion. That makes the US market several hundred times busier.

blocks.q: Why do dealers quote two prices?
blocks.a: They buy a little lower than they sell. The gap is their fee for always being ready to trade.

blocks.label: The one idea to keep
blocks.text: The same rise in yields hurts people who hold long bonds or must borrow today, and helps people who will save for years. An 18-year-old paying into EPF is mostly on the winning side over a working life, even on days the headlines call it a crash.

items.q: Does the 10-year bond set your Malaysian home loan rate?
items.a: No. Since 1 August 2022 new floating home loans follow the Standardised Base Rate, which moves only with the OPR. In the US, the 30-year fixed mortgage does track the 10-year Treasury.

items.q: When US yields jump, does the ringgit always fall?
items.a: No. In 2022 the US 10-year rose from 1.52% to 3.88% and the ringgit fell about 12%. In 2026 the 10-year rose 1.12 points and the ringgit stayed between 3.89 and 4.15 (Fed data).

blocks.text: 7. What makes new tickets pay more or less

Why would new tickets suddenly pay RM5 instead of RM4? Think of a tug of war. The central bank's own rate, expected inflation, how many tickets the government must sell, how many buyers turn up, how fast the economy grows, and how much people trust the borrower all pull on the price of a new ticket.

blocks.text: You can see several forces at once in 2026. The Fed hiked in September (force 1). Oil prices kept inflation worries alive, and the bond market expected about 2.4% a year of inflation over ten years (force 2). A $1.99T deficit meant heavy issuance (force 4). blocks.text: So bonds are not simply safe, and not simply dangerous. They protected savers in 2008 and hurt them in 2022. Higher yields today also mean higher income tomorrow: in October 2026 a 10-year US inflation-linked bond paid about 2.6 points above inflation, against about minus 1 point at the end of 2021.

items.q: Why did safe US bond funds lose 13% in 2022?
items.a: Inflation pushed yields up fast, so old tickets were repriced down. The main US bond index returned -13.01%, its worst year since 1976. The previous worst was -2.92% in 1994.

items.q: In 2008 shares crashed. What did bonds do?
items.a: The main US bond index rose 5.24% while the S&P 500 fell 37.0%. Bonds cushion recessions. They failed to in 2022 because the shock was inflation.

blocks.text: The real return: what is left after tax and inflation

Every yield you see quoted, 5.13% on the 10-year or 4.81% on the 2-year (21 October 2026), is nominal. It counts dollars, not what dollars buy. Level 1's "The yardstick problem" called this the rubber ruler. Your real return is what is left after inflation and, for most savers, after tax. The market publishes its own split: on 21 October 2026 the 10-year inflation-linked Treasury yielded 2.76%, so about 2.4 points of the 5.13% was pay for expected inflation.

items: Start with the nominal yield: 5.13% on a 10-year Treasury in October 2026, or $51.30 a year on $1,000.
Take out tax. In a 24% federal bracket about $39 is left. Treasury interest is free of state income tax, but not of federal tax.
Take out inflation. If prices rise 2.4% a year, about what the bond market expects, $24 of that $39 only keeps up with prices. Your real gain is about 1.5% a year.
If inflation turns out higher than expected, the real return drops below zero, even though every payment arrives on time.

items.q: How much could a risk-free 10-year Treasury lose?
items.a: On price alone, about 32% for someone who bought a new 10-year at 8.76% in July 1979 and still held it in September 1981, when yields hit 15.84%. Counting the coupons collected, the loss was about 14%. From 2021 to 2023 a holder lost about 24% on price and about 21% with coupons (models, Fed H.15 data). Risk-free means free of default, not free of price swings.

items.q: Someone bought a 10-year Treasury at 0.625% in 2020. What is it worth now, and did they lose money?
items.a: About $84 per $100 at today's yields with four years left (model). They lose nothing in dollars if they hold to 2030, but they lose buying power: inflation peaked at 9.1% in 2022.

items.q: A bank failed in 2023 holding bonds that never missed a payment. How?
items.a: Its bonds had lost value as yields rose, about $15.1B at SVB, close to its owners' money, and US banks together carried $620B of such losses at the end of 2022 (FDIC). When depositors ran, the paper loss became real.

blocks.label: How governments quietly shrink debt with inflation

blocks.text: This is not theory. In the 1940s the Fed held long-term yields near 2.5% while inflation ran in double digits after the war, quietly shrinking the war debt in real terms. In the 1970s inflation often ran above bond yields. And anyone who bought a 10-year Treasury at its record low closing yield of 0.52% in August 2020 earned about half a percent a year, while US consumer inflation peaked at 9.1% in June 2022.

This is the quietest way governments shrink debt. Keep the nominal yield below inflation for long enough and the real value of the debt melts, paid for by bondholders and savers who only look at the nominal number. Level 1's "The seasons of money" called it financial repression. The cure is the split in step 3: always separate a yield into the part that only keeps up with inflation and the part that is truly yours.

blocks.q: Why did bonds protect people in 2008 but not in 2022?
blocks.a: 2008 was a recession shock, when yields fell and bond prices rose. 2022 was an inflation shock, when yields rose and bond prices fell along with shares.

blocks.text: 11. The government's side, in one page

Why do governments sell tickets at all? Because they spend more than they collect in taxes, and because a safe ticket is useful to everyone else: banks, pension funds and central banks all need something safe to hold. Each new ticket is sold at an auction, where dealers must bid so that every sale is covered. The resale price then works like a vote that never stops. If buyers doubt a government's plans, they pay less for its tickets, yields rise, and the government's own interest bill grows.
That bill is already large. Malaysia's debt service was RM57.3 billion in 2026, about 15.8% of revenue. In the US, net interest passed $1 trillion in fiscal 2026, more than defense.

items.q: How much of Malaysia's tax money goes on interest?
items.a: Debt service was about RM57.3 billion in 2026, about 15.8% of revenue, and is projected near 16% in 2027 (Ministry of Finance). In the US, net interest of about $1.05 trillion in fiscal 2026 was more than defense.

blocks.label: Why the whole system rests on bonds (the backbone test)

blocks.caption: Picture a champagne tower at a wedding. Government bonds are the bottom row of glasses. Every glass above rests on them.

items: The Fed's money rests on them. The Fed creates bank reserves and cash, and the main asset it holds against them is Treasuries: $4.57T of its $6.47T of securities, about 71% (21 October 2026).

They are the financial system's pawnshop ticket. In repo markets, banks and funds hand over Treasuries to borrow cash, often overnight. About $12.6T of US repo was outstanding on an average day in the third quarter of 2025 (Office of Financial Research).
Banks and money funds park cash in them, because rules treat them as the safest liquid asset.

Stablecoins must hold them. Under the GENIUS Act, compliant dollar tokens must be backed by cash-like reserves: deposits, central bank money, government money funds, repo, or Treasuries with 93 days or less left. Short bills are the dominant choice.
Foreign central banks keep their savings in them. That is how the world holds dollars without holding cash.
They set the base price of money. Mortgages, car loans and company loans are priced as the Treasury yield plus a margin for risk.

items.q: Which is bigger, the world's stock market or its bond market?
items.a: Bonds, just: $160.7T against $157.8T of listed shares at the end of 2025 (SIFMA). Many people guess stocks by a mile. A market value is a price tag, so the order can flip in a big sell-off.

items.q: In 1970 US banks owned almost a third of all Treasuries. What do they own now?
items.a: About 7% (2025). Banks moved from lending to the government to lending to households and firms, while foreigners and funds took over.

items.q: Japan cut its US Treasuries by $171B in six months. Did foreigners flee US debt?
items.a: No. Total foreign holdings were $9.33T in August 2026, near the record, and the UK ($1,010B) is now almost level with Japan ($1,068B) (Treasury TIC data). The foreign share fell because everyone else bought even more.

items.q: A private token company holds about $115B of Treasury bills. Where would that rank among countries?
items.a: Around 20th, close to the UAE and Bermuda in the August 2026 TIC table. The figures are two months apart and Tether's is from press reports of its attestation, so treat the rank as rough. A stablecoin issuer now owns more Treasuries than most nations.

blocks.label: How a bond is born: one real US auction

items: Announcement. The Treasury offered $39.0B of a 10-year note with a 4.625% coupon, maturing 15 August 2036, for auction on 7 October 2026.
Bidding. Bids came in for $109.0B, 2.77 times the amount offered. The 25 primary dealers are required to bid for their share every time, so every auction is fully covered by design.
One price for all. Every winner pays the same yield, the highest one accepted: 5.300%, a price of $94.86 per $100. It was the highest yield at a 10-year auction since November 2000.
Who won. Indirect bidders (foreign and domestic investors bidding through dealers) took 79.6%. Direct bidders took 17.0%. The dealers kept only 2.5%, the smallest share in the data.

Settlement on 15 October. Buyers' banks pay, and the money goes up into the Treasury's account at the Fed. If the buyer was a fund or a person, their deposit is gone until the Treasury spends it (Level 2, "Who really creates money", Step 3).

blocks.text: What the Treasury sells changes what happens to your money. Bills, about 22% of tradable debt, are bought heavily by money market funds. From June 2022 to October 2026 those funds pulled $1.97T out of the cash they had parked at the Fed, much of it to buy bills, and that cash came back into bank deposits when the Treasury spent it. Notes and bonds bought by investors from their own bank deposits drain those deposits until the Treasury spends. Level 2, "Who really creates money", Steps 3 and 4, walks through both cases.

blocks.title: Who wins the 10-year auction: share of the bonds sold, 2008 to 2026
blocks.caption: The dealers' job has shifted from buyer to backstop. Indirect bidders, foreign and domestic investors bidding through dealers, now take most of each sale. 2026 is to date.
blocks.source: US Treasury auction results (fiscaldata), 10-year notes including reopenings.

blocks.q: At the October 2026 auction the dealers, who must bid, kept only 2.5%. Is that a good or a bad sign for the Treasury?
blocks.a: Good in the short run. It means investors wanted the bonds at that price, so the backstop was barely needed. The cost was the price itself: the Treasury had to pay 5.30% to get that demand.

blocks.label: Repo: how a bond is pawned overnight

blocks.text: Repo is a loan secured by a bond. You sell a bond for cash today and agree to buy it back tomorrow at a slightly higher price. The difference is the interest. The lender keeps a cushion called a haircut, for example lending $98 against $100 of bonds. Here a hedge fund buys a $100 Treasury and funds it in repo through a dealer, and a money market fund supplies the cash.

rows: $98 repo loan, plus $2 of its own money
It holds a $100 bond with only $2 of its own money. In practice this is usually one leg of a hedged trade (the cash-futures basis trade), not a bare bet
It is the middleman and nets the two
It swapped a bank deposit for a loan backed by a Treasury
Deposits move from the fund to the bond's seller
