blocks.text: The US repo market had about $12.6T of loans outstanding on an average day in the third quarter of 2025 (Office of Financial Research). That is why a Treasury is worth more than its coupons: it can be turned into cash overnight at a small haircut. It is also where the system breaks. When haircuts jump or dealers run out of room, funds must sell bonds, prices fall, haircuts rise again. That loop drove March 2020.

items.q: Why is a Treasury worth more than the interest it pays?
items.a: Because it is a pawnshop ticket. About $12.6T was outstanding in US repo on an average day in late 2025, mostly against Treasuries. Being able to turn a bond into cash overnight is worth something, so investors accept a slightly lower yield for it.

items.q: Why would the Fed buy more Treasuries in five weeks than it owned in total in 2007?
items.a: In March and April 2020 even Treasuries froze as everyone sold to raise cash. The Fed bought $1.27T in five weeks, against total Treasury holdings of $0.75T at the end of 2007 (Fed H.4.1).

blocks.label: Duration and convexity: the bond's lever

blocks.text: Duration is the number that tells you how hard a bond swings. Roughly, a bond's price moves by its duration, in percent, for each one point move in yields, the other way. It is also about the average time until you get your money back, with near payments counting more than far ones. A 2-year Treasury has a duration near 2, a 10-year near 8, a 30-year near 15.

Look at the last two columns. For the same one point move, the gain when yields fall is bigger than the loss when they rise: +16.8% against -13.4% on the 30-year. That bend is called convexity. It is why long bonds are loved in a crash and feared in an inflation. Duration figures are a model computed for this chapter with half-yearly coupons. Coupons for the 2-year and 30-year are illustrative, the 10-year is the real note auctioned on 7 October 2026.

blocks.label: The yield curve, and the bond market as a voter

blocks.caption: One move in the 10-year yield, four ripples.

blocks.text: Take a $400,000 mortgage over 30 years. At 6.40% the monthly payment is about $2,502. At 7.40%, one point higher, it is about $2,770. One point on the bond market costs that family about $267 a month, about $3,210 a year, for thirty years.

blocks.caption: The yield curve: yields lined up from short to long. Normal curves slope up. An inverted curve, drawn here as an example, often warns of a slowdown.

blocks.text: Line up yields from short to long and you get the yield curve. Normally it slopes up, because waiting longer deserves more pay. In October 2026 it does: about 4.81% at 2 years, 5.13% at 10 years and 5.42% at 30 years. When short yields rise above long ones (an inverted curve), markets are betting the Fed will have to cut, usually because a slowdown is coming. Inversions have come before many US recessions, though the timing is loose. The longest inversion of the 2s and 10s on record, 541 trading days from April 2022 to September 2024, has not been followed by a recession so far, and by 22 October 2026 the curve sloped up again by 0.31 points.

blocks.myth: Government bonds are safe, so you cannot lose money on them.
blocks.reality: They are safe from default, not from price changes. In 2022 bonds had one of their worst years on record. In March 2023 Silicon Valley Bank failed largely because the long Treasuries and mortgage bonds it held had fallen in price as rates rose. Safe means the promise will be kept, not that the price will hold.

blocks.text: I used to think if there was reincarnation, I wanted to come back as the president or the pope or as a .400 baseball hitter. But now I would want to come back as the bond market. You can intimidate everybody.
blocks.by: James Carville, adviser to President Clinton, 1993

blocks.text: The bond market is a voter that votes every second. When it dislikes a government's plans, yields rise and the government's own interest bill rises with them. US net interest reached $1,051.8B in FY2026, more than defense. That bill is the bond market's running verdict, and it is why Treasury secretaries watch auctions more closely than polls.

blocks.text: Here is a Level 2 surprise. At the end of August 2026 Malaysia could borrow for ten years at 3.985%, about 0.8 points cheaper than the United States. blocks.q: New tickets pay RM5. Your RM4 ticket has 10 years left. Roughly what is it worth, and why?

blocks.q: What does the dealer's gap between its buy and sell price tell you in a crisis?
blocks.a: It widens when everyone wants out. A jumping gap is one of the tracks a real alarm leaves.

blocks.q: Which of the three people in this chapter is a bond crash headline really about, and why?
blocks.a: Linda. Her bond fund moves with the 10-year every day and she may need the money soon. Aisyah gains over time through EPF, and the Rahmans feel it only through the OPR and the ringgit.

blocks.q: A bond yields 5% and inflation is 4%. You pay 24% tax on the interest. What is your real return?

chapters.title: Who really creates money: banks, the Fed and the Treasury
chapters.kicker: Bank loans are one door, the busiest one in normal years. Level 2 adds the others: the Fed, the Treasury, the sponges that soak money up, the shredders that destroy it, the brakes on each printer, and how other countries do it.

blocks.label: In 60 seconds
items: Money lives on two floors. Upstairs, banks and the Treasury hold accounts at the Federal Reserve. Downstairs, you and every business hold bank deposits. You can only spend the downstairs kind.

In normal years banks create most new downstairs money when they lend (1971 to 2007, 87% to 96% of the two printers combined). They also create it when they buy a bond or anything else from someone who is not a bank. In 2008 to 2014 and 2020 to 2021 the Fed did most of it.

The Fed creates upstairs money, called reserves, every time it buys a bond. Whether new downstairs money appears too depends on who sold the bond: a bank (no) or a pension fund or other nonbank (yes).
The Treasury moves money between the floors. Selling bonds and collecting taxes pulls deposits up into its Fed account. Spending pushes them back down.
So money is not created only by bank loans. In 2020 and 2021 the Treasury and the Fed together created most of the $4.7 trillion rise in bank deposits.
The Fed is not allowed to buy new bonds straight from the Treasury. It must buy in the open market, through 25 primary dealers.
In short: banks are the everyday printer. The government and the Fed together are the emergency printer, and when both switch it on, as in 2020, it is bigger than anything the banks do.

From 1971 to 2026, bank loans grew about $13.79T and the Fed's bonds about $6.43T: two thirds downstairs, one third upstairs, with the upstairs third arriving in two bursts, 2008 to 2014 and 2020 to 2021.

items.d: Banks' own accounts at the Fed. Upstairs money. About $2.97 trillion on 21 October 2026. Only banks and a few institutions can hold them.
The money in your bank account. Downstairs money, a promise from your bank. About $19.6 trillion at US commercial banks.
The government's checking account at the Fed. About $945 billion on 21 October 2026. Money in it is out of public hands.
One of 25 big dealers that must bid at every Treasury auction and that trade directly with the Fed.
The market where bonds already issued change hands. The only place the Fed may buy Treasuries.
A bank's assets, each scaled by how risky the rules say it is. Capital rules ask for owners' money of at least a set share of this total.

blocks.text: Two floors of money

Picture the dollar system as a building with two floors. Upstairs are the Fed's books. Banks hold reserves there, the Treasury holds its account there, and money funds can park cash there overnight. Downstairs are the public's books: deposits at banks, plus paper cash. When you pay rent or buy groceries, you move downstairs money. Banks settle with each other upstairs.

blocks.label: Picture this
blocks.text: Think of a big market hall. Upstairs is the wholesale floor, where only licensed traders deal, and they settle in special tokens issued by the hall's owner, the Fed. Downstairs is the shop floor, where everyone shops with receipts issued by the traders, which are bank deposits. Some deals happen only upstairs, between traders and the owner. Some happen only downstairs. And some go through the staircase and change the amount of receipts on the shop floor. This chapter is a guide to the staircase.

blocks.q: Can a family spend bank reserves at a shop?
blocks.a: No. Reserves are accounts at the Fed that only banks and a few institutions hold. A family spends deposits or cash. Reserves only matter to the family when a move also changes deposits.

blocks.text: Step 1. Banks create deposits, and not only by lending

When a bank lends you $100, it adds a $100 loan to its assets and a $100 deposit to its debts at the same moment. New downstairs money appears. When you repay, both disappear. That is Level 1 chapter 6. The second way is less known. When a bank buys a $100 bond from a pension fund, it pays by crediting the fund's account with a new $100 deposit. No loan was made, but money was created all the same. When a bank sells a bond to a nonbank, money is destroyed.
Whenever a bank makes a loan, it simultaneously creates a matching deposit in the borrower's bank account, thereby creating new money.
blocks.by: Bank of England, Money creation in the modern economy, 2014

items: A bank lends $100 to a household: the household's deposit rises $100. New money.
The household repays: the deposit and the loan both shrink $100. Money destroyed.
A bank buys a $100 bond from a pension fund: the fund's deposit rises $100. New money without a loan.
Upstairs, nothing changed in total. Reserves only move between banks when the money is spent at another bank.

blocks.q: Your bank buys a building from a developer for $1 million and pays into the developer's account at the same bank. Did the money supply change?
blocks.a: Yes, it rose by $1 million. The bank gained an asset (the building) and a new deposit liability (the developer's balance). Any purchase by a bank from a nonbank creates a deposit.

blocks.text: Step 2. The Fed creates reserves when it buys, and the seller decides the rest

The Fed holds $4.57 trillion of Treasuries. It got them by buying in the open market from the 25 primary dealers, paying with reserves it creates on the spot, and by rolling over bonds as they mature. That is real money creation, but upstairs. Whether it reaches downstairs depends on who sold the bond in the end.

cols: Who sells the bond to the Fed
rows: No change. The bank swapped a bond for reserves.
A pension fund, insurer, money fund or foreign investor
Up $100. The seller's bank gets reserves and credits the seller's deposit.
A dealer selling from its own stock
Up $100 at first. If the dealer uses the cash to repay a loan from a bank, the deposit disappears again.

blocks.text: The primary dealer in the middle is only the pipe. Many of the 25 primary dealers belong to big banking groups, and many act for customers. To know whether a Fed purchase added money you can spend, follow the cash to whoever holds it at the end. In 2020 to 2022 much of the selling came from nonbanks, which is why quantitative easing then added deposits as well as reserves.

blocks.q: The Fed buys $1 billion of Treasuries, and the sellers turn out to be three banks. How much new money can the public spend?
blocks.a: None directly. Bank reserves rose $1 billion, which is upstairs money. Public deposits change only if the sellers are nonbanks, or later when banks spend or lend.

blocks.text: Step 3. The Treasury moves money between the floors

The Treasury keeps its account at the Fed, upstairs. When a fund buys a new Treasury bond at auction, the fund's deposit falls, its bank's reserves fall, and the Treasury's account rises. Money has gone upstairs. When the Treasury pays a Social Security check, the reverse happens: the account falls, and the retiree's deposit and the bank's reserves rise. Taxes work like an auction: deposits go up the stairs. You can watch it happen. In the week to 21 October 2026, on weekly averages, the Treasury's account rose $69 billion and bank reserves fell $60 billion.

blocks.caption: Auctions and taxes lift money into the Treasury's account at the Fed. Spending sends it back down. A deficit means more goes down than comes up.

blocks.text: So does a budget deficit create money? It depends on who buys the new bonds. In fiscal 2026 the deficit was $1.99 trillion.

None overall. The deposits taken at auction come back when the Treasury spends. The buyers now hold a bond instead.

The Fed, indirectly, buying later from nonbanks

blocks.a: Nothing overall. The fund's deposit fell $100 at the auction, and the Treasury's spending added $100 to someone else's deposit. The private sector holds $100 more in bonds, not more money.

Sources: Fed H.8 (banks), H.4.1 (the Fed), H.6 (M2), Treasury Monthly Statement (deficits). Memo, not a deposit flow: the federal deficit was $0.98T (2019), $5.90T (2020 to 2021), $3.07T (2022 to 2023) and $1.99T (fiscal 2026). Whether it added money depends on who bought the bonds (Step 3). The rows do not add exactly to the result, because some channels have no clean series: banks buying back their own shares, fees and interest, and foreign official purchases. In 2019 bank lending and bank bond buying explain the whole rise. In 2020 to 2021 the Fed's channel was 6.6 times bank lending. In 2022 to 2023 deposits fell even though banks lent $1.56T, because QT, bank bond sales and a rising Treasury account drained more.

items.q: In 2020 and 2021 bank deposits rose $4.71T while bank loans rose only $0.68T. Who printed the rest?
items.a: The emergency printer. The Fed bought $4.52T of bonds and banks bought $1.86T of securities while the Treasury ran $5.90T of deficits (Fed H.8 and H.4.1, Treasury statements).

blocks.q: The Fed buys $100 of bonds from a pension fund. What rises upstairs, and what rises downstairs?
blocks.a: Upstairs, bank reserves rise $100. Downstairs, the fund's deposit rises $100. From a bank seller, only the reserves would rise.

blocks.q: A household repays a $100 bank loan. What happens to the money supply?
blocks.a: It falls $100. The loan and the deposit both disappear.

blocks.q: In 2020 to 2021 bank deposits rose $4.71T. How much came from new bank loans, and what did most of the rest?
blocks.a: Only $0.68T. Most of the rest came from the emergency printer: Treasury spending, with the Fed buying $4.52T of bonds and banks buying $1.86T of securities.

blocks.text: Part 2 of 3. Sponges, shredders, brakes and other printers
Step 4. Drains, sponges and new pipes

items: The overnight reverse repo facility: money funds can lend cash to the Fed overnight. While it sits there, it is out of the banks. It peaked at about $2.4 trillion in late September 2022. On 21 October 2026 it held $0.2 billion, so this drain is empty.
The Treasury General Account: every rise drains reserves and often deposits, every fall adds them back.

The standing repo facility (since July 2021): a door that works the other way. Banks and dealers can swap Treasuries for new reserves at a set rate whenever they need them, which limits how far short-term rates can spike in a squeeze.

Stablecoins: buying a dollar token moves your deposit to the issuer, who buys Treasury bills. Bank deposits do not grow, and if the bill comes from a bank or the Treasury, they shrink. The token is a new private dollar outside M2.
Interest on reserves: the Fed pays banks interest by creating new reserves, about $115 billion a year at current rates (desk estimate). Deposits grow only if banks pass it on.

Fed profits and losses: when the Fed earns more than it pays, it sends the profit to the Treasury. From late 2022 it paid more than it earned and built up a $245.9 billion IOU to itself by January 2026. That IOU is now shrinking ($232.7 billion), so it again earns slightly more than it pays, and payments to the Treasury restart once the IOU is cleared. The 'taxes go to the Fed's owners' story has it backwards.

blocks.q: A money fund pulls $50 billion out of the Fed's reverse repo facility to buy new Treasury bills, and the Treasury spends the cash. What happens downstairs?
blocks.a: Deposits rise about $50 billion. The cash was upstairs at the Fed, it passed through the Treasury's account, and the spending landed in public accounts.

blocks.text: The puzzle of the missing shrinkage

cols: Reverse repo (money funds' cash at the Fed)

blocks.text: From June 2022 to October 2026 the Fed's bonds fell $2.01T, yet bank reserves fell only $0.39T. Where did the shrinkage go? Into the sponge. Money funds pulled $1.97T out of the Fed's reverse repo pool to buy Treasury bills, and the cash came back into the banks as the Treasury spent it. QT mostly emptied the sponge, not the banks. Now the sponge is dry, so any further drain hits bank reserves one for one. That is a large part of why the Fed stopped shrinking its Treasuries in December 2025 and has added $0.34T since.
The shredders: six ways money is destroyed

items: Repaying a bank loan. The loan and the deposit both vanish.
Paying taxes. The deposit goes upstairs into the Treasury's account and comes back only when the Treasury spends.
Buying a new Treasury at auction with a deposit. The same as taxes, until the Treasury spends.
Fed QT. When a bond the Fed holds matures and the Treasury repays it with money raised from a nonbank, a deposit and reserves both disappear.
A bank selling a bond to a nonbank, or buying back its own shares or bonds. The buyer pays with a deposit, which the bank cancels.
Money moving into the Fed's reverse repo pool. It leaves the banks while it sits there. In 2020 to 2021 the pool rose $1.64T, more than twice the $0.68T of new bank loans in those two years.

items.q: The Fed shrank its bonds by $2.01T from mid 2022, yet bank reserves fell only $0.39T. Where did the shrinkage go?
items.a: Into an empty sponge: money funds drained $1.97T from the Fed's reverse repo pool to buy bills (Fed H.4.1). The sponge is now dry.

items.q: When you pay your taxes, does the money still exist?
items.a: It leaves the public's books and sits upstairs in the Treasury's account at the Fed, $945B on 21 October 2026, until it is spent again.

items.q: The Fed lost money for three years. Did anyone have to rescue it?
items.a: No. It booked an IOU to itself, a deferred asset, which peaked at $245.9B in January 2026 and is now shrinking ($232.7B). It is earning slightly more than it pays again.

blocks.text: Why the Fed cannot just buy from the Treasury

Section 14 of the Federal Reserve Act says US government bonds may be bought "only in the open market". Congress added that rule in 1935 so that the Treasury would have to face market buyers and could not finance itself at its own central bank. A wartime exception from 1942 allowed up to $5 billion of direct purchases. It was renewed several times, last in 1979, and lapsed in 1981. The Fed can still roll over bonds it already owns by taking new ones at auction, which gives the Treasury no new cash.

A ban on direct buying is not a ban on financing. From 1942 to 1951 the Fed promised to keep bill rates at 0.375% and long bond yields under 2.5%, buying whatever the market sold at those prices. That financed the war debt cheaply without a single direct purchase. The Treasury-Fed Accord of 4 March 1951 ended the deal.
The brakes on each printer

rows: Capital rules: owners' money of at least 4.5% of risk-weighted assets plus buffers. Liquidity rules: enough safe assets for 30 days of stress. Reserve requirement: 0% since 26 March 2020
Borrowers must want loans and pass checks. A loan must beat the bank's funding cost, which the Fed anchors by paying 3.90% on reserves
May buy Treasuries only in the open market (Federal Reserve Act section 14, since 1935). Its mandate: maximum employment, stable prices, moderate long-term rates
Inflation. Buying bonds while inflation runs high fights its own mandate. The current chair calls QE a tool to use sparingly, if at all
Congress must approve spending. The debt limit caps total debt
Auctions must clear. The bond market sets the price, and net interest passed $1T in fiscal 2026
Both keys must turn: Congress spends, the Fed buys from nonbanks
Inflation and the bond market. 2020 to 2021 shows how fast it runs when both keys turn

blocks.text: Notice the reserve requirement: zero since March 2020. The old textbook picture of banks lending out each deposit ten times over has no legal base in the US today. What stops banks is owners' capital, liquidity rules, the price of money and borrowers who must repay. What stops the emergency printer is a law that makes the Fed shop in the open market, a mandate that puts inflation first, and the bond market's price.

items.q: US banks have had to hold zero reserves since March 2020. So what stops them lending forever?
items.a: Capital rules (owners' money absorbs losses), liquidity rules, the 3.90% the Fed pays on reserves, which sets the cost of money, and borrowers who must want and repay loans.

items.q: The Fed has been banned from buying bonds straight from the Treasury since 1935. How did it end up with more than half of the new debt of 2020 and 2021?
items.a: It bought in the open market from dealers and investors, days or months after the auctions. In wartime, 1942 to 1951, it got the same result by capping yields.

blocks.text: Money outside the banks

rows: Retail funds yes, institutional funds no
about $12.6T outstanding on an average day (Q3 2025)
Dollars borrowed outside the US by non-US firms and governments (eurodollars)

blocks.text: Who prints the $14 trillion of dollars borrowed outside America? Bond investors hold over half of it (55% at the end of September 2025, BIS). The rest is loans written by banks abroad, in London, Singapore or Kuala Lumpur, which create dollar loans and deposits on their own books exactly as a US bank does. They settle through accounts at US banks, and in a crisis they need dollars from the Fed's swap lines. So the Fed is the last-resort supplier, while private foreign banks and bond markets are the everyday sources of offshore dollars.

items.q: Money market funds hold $7.98T, about 40% as much as all US bank deposits. Is that money?
items.a: Partly. Retail funds are counted in M2, institutional funds are not, and both are mostly lent to the government. They work like money for their owners, but they rest on Treasuries and on bank deposits.

items.q: Who prints the dollars borrowed outside America?
items.a: Mostly banks and bond markets abroad, about $14T at the end of September 2025 (BIS). The Fed steps in only in a crisis, through swap lines with other central banks.

rows: EU Treaty Article 123 bans direct purchase of government debt
Barred from underwriting new bonds without the Diet's approval
Central bank credit to the government is limited by law
Large loans to banks (mostly repaid now)

The currency door: buying dollars creates ringgit, selling dollars destroys it

blocks.text: The two-floor picture works everywhere, but the doors differ. In Malaysia a large share of changes in central bank money comes through the currency door: when Bank Negara buys dollars to steady the ringgit, it pays with new ringgit reserves, then usually soaks them back up. In Japan the central bank owns so much of the bond market that who sold a bond matters less than how much the Bank of Japan chose to buy.

items.q: When Bank Negara buys dollars to steady the ringgit, does it create ringgit?
items.a: Yes, at first: it pays with new ringgit reserves. It then usually soaks them back up in its money market operations, so the ringgit money stock need not change.

items.q: The Bank of Japan owns about half of its government's bonds. Who is the printer in Japan?
items.a: The central bank, on a scale no other big economy matches. It held about 47% of government bonds, excluding bills, in June 2026, after its share first fell below 50% at the end of 2025, for the first time since 2022 (Ministry of Finance).

blocks.q: US banks have had no reserve requirement since March 2020. Name two things that still stop them lending without limit.
blocks.a: Any two of: capital rules, liquidity rules, the 3.90% the Fed pays on reserves, and borrowers who must want and repay loans.

blocks.text: Part 3 of 3. Who printed, year by year, and what the critics say
What the critics add

cols: What it adds to this chapter
rows: Treat the Fed and the Treasury as one. The state spends first, taxes and bond sales drain afterwards. The limit is inflation, not money

Deficit spending is the only source of net financial assets for the non-government sector as a whole, which means the domestic private sector plus foreigners (Stephanie Kelton, The Deficit Myth, 2020). A country's private sector can also gain them from a trade surplus.
New money enters unevenly. The first receivers, banks and asset owners, gain before prices rise. Credit without savings breeds booms that end in busts
Ask who receives new money first, not only which floor it lands on (Murray Rothbard, The Case Against the Fed, 1994)
The quantity of money matters for inflation, with a lag of one to two years
M2 rose about 40% in 2020 to 2021 and inflation peaked at 9.1% in June 2022. Then M2 fell in 2022 and 2023 (Tim Congdon, 2025)
Central banks set the price of money. Banks and borrowers choose the quantity
QE works mainly through bond yields and portfolios, not only through the deposit count

blocks.text: We found no school whose strongest objection points to a channel missing from this chapter. Each points to a missing consequence. The Austrian asks who got the money first. The monetarist asks what it did to prices. The MMT economist asks why we pretend the Treasury needs to borrow its own currency. A complete Level 2 reader can hold all three questions at once.

items.q: M2 fell in 2022 and 2023, the first full-year falls since the record starts in 1959. Why was there no deflation?
items.a: Prices respond with a lag, and the stock of money was still about 35% to 40% above early 2020. Inflation slowed but stayed positive.

items.q: Is today's two-printer system the old empire habit of debasing money, or a safeguard against it?
items.a: Both readings have evidence. M2 grew about 37 times since 1970 (Fed H.6). But the open market rule, the 1951 Accord and the 2022 to 2023 contraction show a brake that empires lacked.

blocks.text: Putting sizes on it

blocks.caption: Every channel that creates or destroys the public's deposits, with rough sizes for the latest year and for 2020 to 2021.

blocks.text: In an ordinary year, bank lending is the biggest engine. In the pandemic it was the government and the central bank: the Treasury spent borrowed money straight into household accounts, and the Fed and banks ended up holding about 68% to 72% of the new bonds, so nothing drained the deposits back. M2 rose about 40% in two years, from $15.5 trillion in February 2020 to $21.7 trillion in February 2022.

blocks.myth: All money is created by banks making loans.
blocks.reality: Loans are the main channel in normal years (87% to 96% of the two printers from 1971 to 2007), but banks also create money when they buy securities, the Fed creates reserves whenever it buys and deposits when the seller is a nonbank, and Treasury spending adds deposits unless the public funded it from its own accounts. In 2020 to 2021 the Treasury and Fed channel created most new deposits.

blocks.myth: The Fed prints money and hands it to the government.
blocks.reality: The Fed may not lend to the Treasury or buy at auction. It buys bonds from dealers in the open market and pays the sellers. That holds down yields and can turn bonds held by the public into deposits, which finances deficits indirectly. Its profits go back to the Treasury, and since 2022 it has been running losses.

blocks.text: So who is printing? The everyday printer and the emergency printer

Put all of this together. In a normal year, banks are the main printer: new spendable money appears mostly because people and firms borrow. In the year to September 2026, bank loans grew by about $1.0 trillion and deposits by about $1.2 trillion. But the government and the Fed together can do the same job, and in some years they do it far more than the banks. That combination is printing money in everything but name.

blocks.caption: Two ways new spendable money is made. The banks run every day. The government and the Fed switch on in emergencies, and then they are bigger.

items: The government spends more than it collects in taxes. When it pays a salary, a pension or a stimulus check, a new deposit lands in someone's bank account. Spending is what actually puts the money in public hands.
To cover the gap, the Treasury sells bonds.

Whether new money is left over depends on who ends up holding those bonds. If households and funds buy them with savings they already had, money only moves around and nothing new is left. If banks buy them, or the Fed buys them in the market from dealers and pension funds, the public keeps the new deposits and the bonds sit with the banks or the Fed. New money remains.

No. Money moves to the government and comes back

blocks.label: Picture this
blocks.text: Think of two printers in an office. The banks' printer runs all day, printing a little each time someone signs a loan, and it shreds the pages again as loans are paid back. The government and the Fed share a second printer kept in a locked room. It needs two keys: Congress must approve the spending, and the Fed must choose to buy the bonds. When both keys turn, as in 2020, it prints faster than anything the banks can do.

The clearest case is 2020 to 2021. Bank deposits jumped $4.7 trillion, about 36% (December 2019 to December 2021). Most of it came from government spending on stimulus checks, business support loans and unemployment benefits, while the Fed ended up with about 56% to 59% of the new marketable Treasury debt, depending on the source. Bank loans rose only $0.68 trillion, a seventh of the deposit rise.
Then why do people say the government cannot just print?

items: The Fed decides, not the Treasury. The law lets the Fed buy only in the open market, for its own reasons such as interest rates or market stability, and it can stop or reverse. Since 2022 it has been shrinking its bond holdings, which pulls money back out.

The bond market votes. If investors think a government is leaning on the printer, they demand higher interest rates. That is part of why the US 10-year yield is near 5% and the interest bill passed $1 trillion a year.
There is friction. Congress must approve the spending, the debt ceiling has to be dealt with, and every auction has to find buyers.

blocks.text: The two kinds of money behave differently over time. Bank-loan money is temporary: when the loan is repaid, the money disappears. Deficit money can stay, because the government rarely pays its debt down overall and rolls the bonds over. So the old worry that governments finance themselves by creating money is right when banks or the Fed end up holding the bonds, as in 2020 to 2021 (about 68% to 72% of the new debt). It is wrong when savers buy the bonds with money they already had.

blocks.q: In 2020 bank deposits rose by trillions while bank lending barely grew. Which printer was running, and what two things had to happen?
blocks.a: The emergency printer. The government had to spend far more than it taxed, and the Fed and banks had to end up holding much of the new debt. Together that left trillions of new deposits in public hands.

blocks.text: Fifty-five years of money creation: downstairs banks versus the upstairs printer, 1971 to 2026

Since the dollar left gold in 1971, how much new money came from banks lending, and how much from the Fed buying bonds upstairs? The chart below puts the two printers side by side for every year, using the Federal Reserve's own data. The gold bars are the yearly change in commercial bank loans. The blue bars are the yearly change in the bonds the Fed holds (Treasuries plus mortgage bonds). The dots are the actual change in the money supply (M2).

blocks.caption: Yearly change in commercial bank loans (gold) and in the Fed's bond holdings (blue), with the change in M2 (dots), 1971 to 2026. Bars below the line mean that printer was shrinking. 2026 runs to September for loans, 21 October for the Fed and August for M2.

items: 1971 to 2007: the banks did almost all of it. In every decade the Fed's share of the two printers was only 4% to 13%. Its bond buying in those years was about the size of the paper cash people came to hold: the Fed's bonds rose about $0.72T from 1971 to 2007, and currency in circulation was about $0.83T at the end of 2007.
2008 to 2014: the first emergency. Bank loans actually fell by $481 billion in 2009, while the Fed bought bonds worth $3.44T over the period. Upstairs took about 75% of the work.
2015 to 2019: the banks took over again, adding $2.43T of loans while the Fed shrank its holdings by about $449B.
2020 to 2021: the biggest switch-on ever. The Fed bought $4.52T of bonds against $681B of new bank loans, about 87% upstairs. M2 jumped $6.15T in two years, the fastest rise in the record.

2022 to 2025: the printer ran backwards. The Fed shrank its bonds by about $2.00T while banks lent $2.60T. M2 rose only $853B over four years, and fell in 2022 and 2023, the first full-year falls in the official M2 record, which starts in 1959.
2026 so far: both printers are adding again, banks about $784B and the Fed about $201B.

The whole period: banks added about $13.79T of loans and the Fed about $6.43T of bonds. Roughly two thirds downstairs and one third upstairs, but the upstairs third came in two short bursts. M2 grew from about $0.63 trillion at the end of 1970 to about $23.3 trillion in August 2026, roughly 37 times.

blocks.text: How to read the bars fairly. They are the two main engines, not a complete accounting, so they do not add up exactly to the change in M2. Banks also create deposits by buying Treasuries themselves (about $1.9 trillion over the period), the Treasury's cash balance at the Fed swings up and down, and people move money in and out of cash. The blue bar is also the upper limit of upstairs money reaching the public, because Fed buying adds spendable deposits only when the seller is not a bank. Bank loans here are commercial banks only.

blocks.q: Looking at the chart, in which two periods did the upstairs printer do most of the work, and what happened to the money supply right after the second one?
blocks.a: 2008 to 2014 and 2020 to 2021. After 2021 the Fed shrank its bonds by about $2 trillion, and M2 fell in 2022 and 2023 for the first time in the official record.

rules: Ask which floor moved. Reserves are money for banks. Deposits are money for you.
The Fed creates reserves whenever it buys. It creates spendable deposits only when the seller is not a bank.
Auctions and taxes pull money up into the Treasury's account. Spending pushes it back down.
A deficit adds to your money only if banks, the Fed or parked cash fund it.
Banks create money by lending and by buying. Repayments and sales destroy it.
Banks are the everyday printer. The government plus the Fed is the emergency printer.
Before you say who printed money, name the year: banks in normal years, the government plus the Fed in emergencies.
Watch the sponges. When the reverse repo pool is empty, every drain hits bank reserves directly.

chapters.title: The world's balance sheet: what it owns, what it owes, and how countries are built
chapters.kicker: You may have heard that the world owes $300 trillion, or $500 trillion, or more. Each can be true, depending on what you count, and the world owes all of it to itself. This chapter shows what the world really owns, why its debts cancel but still matter, how the numbers grew, and how each big country is built.

items: Which debt? On the usual meaning, loans and bonds, the world owes about $348T (end 2025) to over $365T (mid 2026, IIF, via press). Its net wealth is about $518T (UBS, households) to $600T (McKinsey, all sectors, via press). Count everything owed on paper, deposits and other claims included, and the debt side is about $1,200T (computed from McKinsey).

You cannot subtract one from the other. Every debt is somebody's asset, so at world level the debts cancel. What is left is real things, about two thirds of them real estate (McKinsey's 2021 study, Level 1).
The debts cancel for the world, not for each family. Who owes whom, in which currency, and how soon decides the danger.
In 2025 about four fifths of the rise in household wealth was higher prices and inflation, and about a fifth was new investment (McKinsey, via press).

Debt grew from about 1 year of world output in 1971 (a model estimate) to about 2.5 years (3 counting the financial sector's own debts). It jumps in crises, 2008 and 2020. After 2020 the debt ratio fell while dollar debt kept rising, except in 2022, when a strong dollar shrank it.
The dollar is the ruler. Japan's debt fell by a third in dollars from 2020 to 2025 while it rose in yen. Nobody repaid anything.

Countries are built differently. The US is the richest country and the largest net debtor to the world. Japan's state owes mostly its own central bank and savers (foreigners about 13%). Italian families owe little (36% of output) while their state owes 137%. China borrowed to grow and saved at home.

Part 1 of 3. What the world owns and owes
The question that started this chapter

If the world wealth is 300T+ and 500T+ world debt, now show others a brief timeline of how others, maybe the G7 or G10, are different in structure, so users can understand and quantify the numbers around the world.
blocks.by: The owner of this guide, October 2026 (lightly edited)

blocks.text: It is a sharp question, and the honest answer starts with a question back: which debt? Both numbers can be true, depending on what you count. Count loans and bonds, the usual meaning of debt, and the world owes about $348 trillion to $365 trillion, while its net wealth is about $518 trillion to $600 trillion. On that count the order in the question flips. Count everything owed on paper by every part of the world, bank deposits and other claims included, and the total is about $1,200 trillion, far above $500 trillion. So "300T+" is right as a floor for wealth, and "500T+" is too high for loans and bonds and too low for everything owed. One thing holds on every count: none of these debts can be subtracted from wealth, because the world owes all of them to itself. The words below come first, then the numbers.

blocks.label: Seven words to pin down first

items.d: What you own minus what you owe. A $500k house, $100k of savings and a $300k mortgage make $300k.
The net wealth of a whole country or the world, all sectors together.
A claim on someone else: a deposit, a bond, a loan, a share. One side's asset is the other side's debt.
Every IOU counted once, from the borrower's side, with nothing subtracted.
Debt of governments, firms and households only. The financial sector's own borrowing is left out, so the same lending is not counted twice: a bank borrows in order to lend to the other three.
World totals are in dollars. When the dollar moves 10%, non-US numbers move about 10% with nothing real changing.
What a country owns abroad minus what it owes abroad, shares and firms included. It is not the same as foreign debt.

The financial firms of the world, central banks, banks and other funds, held $503.7 trillion of financial assets at the end of 2024 (Financial Stability Board). That is a count of claims. It includes much of the world's debt seen from the lender's side, plus shares and claims on each other.
People's net wealth: $517.7 trillion at the end of 2025 (UBS). The number may simply belong on the other side of the ledger.
Everything owed on paper by every sector: about $1,200 trillion (computed from McKinsey). On that count "500T+" is true, more than twice over.

Derivatives: over-the-counter contracts with a notional value of $846 trillion at the end of June 2025 (BIS). Notional is the size of the thing bet on, not money owed. Their gross market value, closer to what is actually at stake, was $21.8 trillion. Never add notional derivatives to debt.

blocks.label: Popular claim
blocks.text: "The world owes $500 trillion and is only worth $300 trillion." What it gets right: the world's paper claims are enormous, and on the widest count of everything owed (about $1,200 trillion) they are far bigger than $500 trillion. What it gets wrong: on the usual meaning of debt, loans and bonds, the world owes about $348 trillion to $365 trillion, while its net wealth is $518 trillion to $600 trillion. And on any count the two cannot be subtracted, because the world owes all of it to itself.

blocks.text: Every one of these numbers comes from a different counter with a different purpose. UBS counts people's wealth for a wealth manager's report. The IIF is a bank industry body and counts the financial sector's own debts, so its figure is the biggest of the usual debt counts. The FSB counts financial firms' assets to watch for risk. McKinsey counts every balance sheet, which is how it reaches nearly $1,800 trillion. When two headlines disagree, first ask which counter they used.

Two kinds of pension sit in different places. Private pension funds are inside household wealth: the savings belong to people. Unfunded state promises, such as public pensions and health care paid from future taxes, are in none of these debt counts. They are real claims on future taxpayers, and hard-money writers often add them to debt. This chapter does not, and has no checked figure for them yet.
The great cancellation: why the world cannot owe anyone outside itself

Every debt has two sides. When a family owes a bank $300,000, the bank owns a $300,000 claim. When the US Treasury owes $1,000 on a bond, a pension fund, a bank, the Fed or a foreign central bank owns that claim. Add up every balance sheet on Earth and each IOU appears once as a debt and once as an asset. They cancel. There is no bank on Mars that the world owes.

Imagine a family of four who lend each other money all year: the teenager owes the parents for a phone, a parent owes the grandmother for a car, the grandmother owes the teenager for help with the shop. At the end of the year the IOUs on the fridge add up to $50,000. Is the family $50,000 poorer? No. The IOUs are owed from one member to another. The family is worth its house, its car and its shop. The IOUs only matter if one member cannot pay another.

The debts cancel for the world, not for each family. Creditors and debtors are different families, so interest flows from one group to another. In the United States, the top 10% of households took 67.5% of the rise in household net worth since the end of 2019, and the bottom half took 3.1% (Federal Reserve distributional accounts, mid 2026).

blocks.text: Inside the US, the government's new debt is the private sector's new asset, so "we owe it to ourselves" is right for that half. The foreign half is a claim of Japan on future US income, and it was created when the US bought more from the world than it sold. That is why only countries, not the world, can owe outside. The US's net foreign position was about minus $26.5 trillion at the end of 2024 (IMF) and minus $27.5 trillion at the end of 2025 (BEA), while Japan's was about plus $3.5 trillion (end 2024). A net foreign position is not the same as foreign debt: part of the US figure is foreigners owning US shares and companies, and stock prices move it a lot (BEA).

So what survives the cancellation? Three things. Real assets: land, houses, offices, factories, machines, roads and software, worth roughly the world's $600 trillion of net worth (McKinsey, via press), about two thirds of it real estate (Level 1, "The titled world"). Assets that are nobody's IOU, like gold bullion and bitcoin, which are small next to property. And, in household wealth only, the market's view of companies' future earnings above what their books show, because shares are counted at market price. In national net worth that extra cancels, because a share is also a claim on the company. World wealth, measured in dollars, is mostly the price of real things.

items.q: If every debt is somebody's asset, who is the world in debt to?
items.a: Itself. The $348T of debt the IIF counts is matched by $348T of claims held by people, pension funds, banks and central banks. Only countries can owe outside: the US's net foreign position was about minus $26.5T at the end of 2024, Japan's about plus $3.5T.

items.q: Why is the richest country also the biggest debtor?
items.a: Because lenders lend against assets and income, and because the world wants dollar assets. The US holds about 35% of world household wealth and owes about 29% of world nonfinancial debt. Its net foreign position, about minus $26.5T at the end of 2024, is part debt and part foreign ownership of US shares and firms, and the US can owe it in its own currency.

blocks.text: Part 2 of 3. How it grew, and how to hold it in your head
Price, not pile

Debt and wealth can both grow at once, for four reasons. A loan that builds a new house adds a debt and a new real asset. A loan that buys an existing house adds a debt and a deposit, and more credit chasing the same houses lifts their price, which shows up as more wealth. Inflation lifts both in dollars. And the two are counted differently: debt is a gross count of IOUs, net worth is what is left after they cancel.

How much of new wealth is new things? McKinsey's 2026 report, as summarized in the press, found that only about 20% of the rise in household wealth in 2025 came from net new investment, and about 58% came from higher valuations above inflation. The rest was inflation itself. The report was not opened for this chapter, so treat the split as approximate. The direction matches Level 1's "The titled world": the same buildings became worth more.

items.a: No. Only about a fifth of the household gain came from new investment, and most of the rest from higher prices. A weaker dollar also lifted the dollar value of non-US wealth.

items.a: Measured wealth falls by roughly 13% of net worth (two thirds times 20%, a model using McKinsey's 2021 finding that real estate is about two thirds of net worth). No house is lost and no debt is repaid. Debt stays at face value, so everyone's debt looks bigger next to what they own.

blocks.text: The ruler moves: the dollar resizes the world

Every world total is counted in dollars. When the dollar rises, everything outside the US looks smaller, and when it falls, everything looks bigger, with nothing real changing. Japan shows how large this effect can be.

rows: As a share of Japan's GDP

blocks.text: Japan's debt rose 3% in yen and fell 32% in dollars, because the yen fell from about 103 to about 157 per dollar. Its debt also fell as a share of its economy, because inflation returned and lifted nominal output. Nobody repaid anything. The same ruler worked the other way in 2025: the euro rose almost 9% against the dollar, which is part of why wealth in Europe, the Middle East and Africa grew about 17.5% in dollars that year (UBS).

In 2022 the ruler worked the other way for the whole world. The dollar rose, and world debt measured in dollars fell about $4 trillion, to just under $300 trillion, the IIF's first annual fall since 2015. World household wealth fell too, about 2.4% to $454.4 trillion on the UBS and Credit Suisse count (via press), as higher interest rates cut asset prices. Nobody repaid anything.

items.q: Japan's debt fell by a third in dollars from 2020 to 2025. Did Japan repay?
items.a: No. In yen it rose 3% (2,273 to 2,340 trillion yen, BIS). The yen fell against the dollar, so the ruler shrank the number.

items.q: World wealth rose 10.8% in dollars in 2025. Measured in ounces of gold, did it rise or fall?
items.a: It fell, by about a third. Gold rose about 66% in 2025 (press), so 1.108 divided by 1.66 is about 0.67 (a model). Neither ruler is the right one alone. Check big claims with more than one ruler.

blocks.text: Three things stand out. Debt grew faster than output in almost every period since 1971, from about one year of world output (a model) to about two and a half. It grew in jumps, in 2008 to 2010 and above all in 2020, when a record $35 trillion was added in one year (IIF). And after 2020 the world ratio fell for years while the dollar amount kept climbing, apart from 2022, when it fell about $4 trillion as a strong dollar shrank everything counted outside the US. Inflation and the ruler did that, not repayment. The fall did not last in dollars: debt rose about $46 trillion from the end of 2024 to mid 2026 ($319.5 trillion to over $365 trillion, IIF), and the BIS ratio rose again in 2025.

This was not the first time. After the Second World War the US and the UK shrank their government debt as a share of output without repaying it, by growing and by keeping interest rates below inflation (Level 1's "The seasons of money", citing Reinhart and Sbrancia, 2011). The years after 2020 were a short replay.

The sources do not always agree on direction. In 2025 the BIS measure of world debt to output rose (235% to 246%) while the IIF's fell (to about 308%). The likely reason is how each converts currencies when the dollar falls during a year. It is a reminder that a single year's move in a world ratio can depend on who is counting.

items.q: The world debt ratio fell for years after 2020 while dollar debt kept climbing. How can both be true, and what happened in 2022?
items.a: Inflation raised nominal output faster than debt. On the BIS measure world nonfinancial debt went from $222T (285% of output) in 2020 to $237T (235%) in 2024. Nobody paid it down. In 2022 dollar debt even fell, by about $4T on the IIF count, because a strong dollar shrank everything measured in dollars outside the US.

items.q: When did world debt jump most: 1971, 2008 or 2020, and who borrowed?
items.a: 2020: a record $35T in one year, with governments borrowing about $14T of it (IIF). In 2008 to 2010 the BIS ratio rose from 202% to 229%. In 1971 there was no jump: debt sat near 100% of world output (IMF).

blocks.label: The US and Japan
blocks.text: The US is the richest country and the largest net debtor to the rest of the world, about minus $26.5T at the end of 2024. It can borrow abroad in its own currency because the world wants dollars. The bigger currency risk in world debt sits outside the US: about $14T of dollar credit owed by borrowers abroad at the end of September 2025 (BIS), which gets heavier for them when the dollar rises. Japan's government owes about twice its output, yet Japan as a nation is owed $3.5T by the world. The Bank of Japan held about 43% of the government's bills and bonds at the end of 2025 (41% by June 2026) and foreigners about 13%, so Japan's debt is mostly owed from one Japanese pocket to another, in yen. Its government debt is 193% of output on the BIS basis, about 207% gross on the IMF's, and about 136% net of the government's own financial assets (IMF). Each figure is right on its own basis. The risk shows up as a weak yen, not as foreign creditors walking away.

blocks.label: Germany and Italy
blocks.text: One currency, opposite structures. Germany's state owes 63% of output, Italy's 137%. Yet the typical Italian adult is richer than the typical German one: median wealth $131,001 against $53,485 (UBS, modelled). Italian families owe little, 36% of output against 48% in Germany. The usual explanation is home ownership, which is more common in Italy, though this chapter has not checked the figures. Italy's state is the debtor, its families much less so. Neither country prints its own currency, so investors can charge either one a risk premium when they worry. Countries with their own central bank pay such premia too, as Britain found in 2022.

blocks.label: France
blocks.text: Same euro, a different worry. The French state owes about 116% of output, less than Italy's 137% (BIS), and French companies carry the heaviest debt in this table, 155% of output. Investors outside France, including other euro area investors and the ECB, hold about 54% of French government debt (Eurostat), and France owes the world a net $0.7T (end 2024). Yet in early October 2026 investors charged France more than Italy to borrow for ten years: about 1.4 points over Germany for France, against about 1.2 for Italy (press). They were reacting to France's deficit and politics more than to the size of its debt. A debt ratio is where the analysis starts, not where it ends.

blocks.label: The UK and Canada
blocks.text: House-rich households with heavy mortgages. Canadian household debt is about 100% of output and British about 74%, among the highest in the G7. When interest rates rise, these families feel it first, because their mortgages reset within a few years. Canada is a large net creditor abroad, partly thanks to big pension funds investing overseas, while the UK is a small net debtor.

blocks.label: Switzerland
blocks.text: A tiny state and heavy private balance sheets. The Swiss government owes only 25% of output, Swiss households 123%, the highest in the table, much of it mortgages that owners often keep rather than repay. Yet Swiss adults are the richest on Earth on average ($910,382) and the country owns far more abroad than it owes. High gross debt, very high net wealth: proof that gross debt alone says little.

blocks.label: China
blocks.text: Debt-built growth, saved at home. China's total nonfinancial debt is about 300% of output, above the US, and its companies, including local government financing vehicles, carry most of it (143%). Yet China is a net creditor abroad, because its savings are lent at home, through Chinese banks, in yuan. Falling property prices have dragged on its household wealth.

blocks.label: Malaysia
blocks.text: A smaller currency with a foreign window. Malaysia's nonfinancial debt is about 224% of output: government 65%, households 70% (high for an emerging market, including mortgages and car loans), companies 89%. It owes the world about as much as it owns abroad. Foreigners hold about a fifth of Malaysian Government Securities (20.1% in July 2026), enough that a jump in US yields can pull money out and push the ringgit down, as Level 1's "The view from a smaller currency" described.

items.q: Japan's government owes about twice its GDP. Why is it not treated like Greece was?
items.a: Its debt is in yen, the Bank of Japan held about 43% of it at the end of 2025, foreigners only about 13%, and Japan as a whole is owed $3.5T by the world. Greece borrowed in a currency it could not print, much of it from foreigners.

items.q: Germany, Italy and France share the euro. Why did France, with less government debt than Italy, pay more to borrow in October 2026?
items.a: Investors price the risk that worries them now, not only the size of the debt. France's deficit and politics worried them more than Italy's higher debt: about 1.4 points over Germany for France against about 1.2 for Italy (press, early October 2026). None of the three can print euros.

items.q: Is a country with high government debt but rich households poor or rich?
items.a: Look at the whole national balance sheet. Japan: state debt 193% of output, yet a net creditor of 83% of output abroad. Switzerland: tiny state debt, households owe 123% of output, still the richest adults on Earth.

items.q: China is not in the G7 or the G10. Why does that change the picture?
items.a: China holds about 16% of world household wealth (18.5% counting Hong Kong and Taiwan) and 22% of world nonfinancial debt, and it added more than $4.8T of the roughly $10T rise in world debt in the first half of 2026 (IIF, via press). Leave it out and you miss nearly half of the rise in world debt in 2026 so far.

blocks.text: Say it back

blocks.q: A friend says the world is $500 trillion in debt and only worth $300 trillion. What would you ask first, and what two things would you tell them?
blocks.a: Ask: which debt? Then, first: on the usual meaning, loans and bonds, the world owes about $348T to $365T and is worth $518T to $600T net, so the order flips. Only the widest count, everything owed on paper including deposits, passes $500T, at about $1,200T. Second: whichever count they mean, it cannot be subtracted from wealth, because the world owes it to itself. What matters is who owes whom, in which currency, and how soon.

blocks.q: Why can Japan owe twice its output and still be a creditor nation?
blocks.a: Its government owes mostly its own central bank, banks, insurers and savers, in yen, while Japan as a whole owns $3.5T more abroad than it owes.

blocks.q: World debt to output fell in 2023 and 2024 while the dollar amount rose. What did the work?
blocks.a: Inflation. Nominal output grew faster than debt, so the ratio fell without anyone paying debt down.

chapters.title: The money clubs: who writes the rules, who can really print, and the game the world plays
chapters.kicker: The G7, G10 and G20 are clubs, not governments. This chapter shows what they can and cannot do, which countries can really print money and which cannot, why Malaysia sits outside every club but inside the game, and five questions that turn the world into a game board.

items: The G7, G10 and G20 are clubs, not governments. They have no treaty, no money and no power to force anyone. They work by asking.
The G20 moves fast in a crisis, when acting together is every member's best move, and slowly in calm years, when each member prefers to let others pay.
Can a country print money? It is a ladder, not a yes or no. Three tests: its own currency, debt owed in that currency, and markets that let it print without a crash.
The US sits at the top. Euro members, Ecuador and Panama cannot print their own money at all. Turkey, Argentina and Sri Lanka could print but paid for it.

Malaysia is in no club, yet lives by the clubs' rules. It sits on rung 3, near the top: 98.8% of its federal debt is owed at home, but a fifth of its bonds sit with foreigners, so its real brake is the ringgit.
Five questions turn the world into a game board: coordination, free riders, the prisoner's dilemma, focal points, self-insurance and runs.

Part 1 of 3. The clubs, and whether they deliver
1. Three clubs, no government

These are clubs, not governments. None has a treaty, a binding vote, its own money or a large permanent staff. They cannot pass a law, print a dollar or force a private lender to do anything. They work through bodies they control: the IMF, the Financial Stability Board, the Basel committee that writes bank rules, and the OECD tax talks. A club statement is a promise. Each member must still pass its own laws.

2. Is the G20 just playing around?
The owner's suspicion is that the G20 is playing around. Here is its record on nine big promises. The grades are our own judgment of the evidence.

Made. The IMF got new money and the world economy grew again in 2010

blocks.text: Score: 2 delivered, 4 partly, 2 not delivered, 1 stalled. So the suspicion is half right. In 2008 and 2009 the G20 moved within months. Since then it has moved slowly, and in 2025 and 2026 it has split in the open. October 2026 is a calm year with a broken club, so the impression fits today. It would not have fitted April 2009.

blocks.label: The game behind the scorecard
blocks.text: In a crisis the G20 plays a coordination game: every member faces the same collapse, so acting together is each member's best move. In calm years it plays free-rider games: each member does best by letting the others pay. A club with no treaty can coordinate the willing. It cannot force the unwilling.

blocks.q: Which club is Malaysia in: the G7, the G10 or the G20?
blocks.a: None. It sits in ASEAN, APEC and the Chiang Mai pool, and is a BRICS partner, but in none of the three money clubs.

blocks.q: Why can a G20 promise be broken without penalty?
blocks.a: The G20 has no treaty, no court and no money of its own. A promise binds only if each member passes its own law.

blocks.q: Why did the G20 move fast in 2009 but slowly on poor countries' debts?
blocks.a: In 2009 every member feared the same collapse, so acting together paid each one. Debt relief by one lender frees cash for the others, so each prefers to let others give it.

blocks.text: Part 2 of 3. Who can really print money
3. Three locks on the printing press

Here printing means a state and its central bank creating the money that the state's debts are owed in. Banks are the other printer, which Level 2 chapter 2 covers. To print freely, a country must open three locks.

items: Lock 1, the law. Does it issue its own currency through its own central bank? Italy, Ecuador and Panama do not. Their money is the euro or the US dollar, made by someone else.

Lock 2, the debt. Does the state owe its debt in the money it can create? A state that owes dollars cannot print dollars. Sri Lanka could print rupees, but it owed dollars, and stopped paying on 12 April 2022.

Lock 3, the market. Can it print a lot in a crisis without its currency crashing or prices taking off? That depends on whether the world wants to hold its money, how open its markets are, and its record on inflation. Turkey and Argentina had their own money and owed much of their debt at home, and still saw inflation reach 72% (2022) and 220% (2024).

blocks.text: Each lock is needed and none is enough on its own. A country that passes lock 1 can always pay a debt in its own money. It cannot choose what that money will buy.
4. The ladder

blocks.caption: Six rungs of printing power. Malaysia sits on rung 3, highlighted, near the top of it.

blocks.text: The rungs are our grading of the evidence, not an official list. Two edges are worth a look. Indonesia's central bank holds about 29% of its government's debt after buying it from 2020 to 2022, and inflation was still 1.9% in 2025: a rung 3 printer can print for a while if markets trust its brakes. Germany sits on rung 5b with the cheapest borrowing in Europe, because markets trust its budget. Rung 5b is a constraint, not a verdict on quality. And the euro area as a whole can print through the ECB, which has promised to support members under conditions.

blocks.q: Sri Lanka had its own currency. Why could it not print its way out in 2022?
blocks.a: Lock 2. Its foreign debts were owed in dollars, and a rupee printer cannot make dollars.

blocks.q: Name one country on rung 5b and say why it is there.
blocks.a: Any euro member, Ecuador or Panama. None issues the money its debts are owed in.

blocks.text: Part 3 of 3. Malaysia, and the game the world plays
5. Malaysia: outside every club, inside the game

Malaysia sits in none of the money clubs. Indonesia is the only Southeast Asian member of the G20. Malaysia's seats are elsewhere: ASEAN, which it helped found in 1967, APEC, the IMF, the Chiang Mai reserve pool with China, Japan and Korea, and since October 2024 a BRICS partner seat. Yet it applies rules written in rooms it is not in. It brought in the 15% global minimum tax from 1 January 2025, the same deal the US, which helped write it, later got a carve-out from.

cols: Who holds Malaysia's federal government debt (end June 2026)

blocks.text: Federal debt was RM1.38 trillion at the end of June 2026, 63.1% of output. 98.8% of it is owed at home, almost all in ringgit (Ministry of Finance). Nearly half, 47.9%, is Islamic paper. Bank Negara holds only 3.8%, against about 29% at Indonesia's central bank. Malaysia has not used its printer to fund the budget.

rows: The ringgit fixed at 3.80 per dollar
The peg ends. A managed float against a basket of currencies begins

blocks.text: Malaysia did not take an IMF programme in 1998, while Thailand, Indonesia and Korea did. Today Bank Negara calls its regime a managed float, and the IMF calls it floating. Both are true: the IMF's floating allows smoothing, which is what Bank Negara means by managing. Offshore ringgit trading is still not allowed.

rows: Central bank holds of government bonds

blocks.text: So Malaysia is typical of its class in most ways: its own currency, a float with smoothing, debt at home, low inflation, a partly managed capital account. It is an outlier in five: the 1998 controls and peg, the highest foreign share of the three ASEAN peers, a compulsory pension fund as its biggest lender, nearly half its debt in Islamic form, and a central bank that holds very little government debt.

blocks.label: Where Malaysia sits
blocks.text: Rung 3, near the top. It opens lock 1 (its own currency) and lock 2 strongly (98.8% of federal debt at home, in ringgit). It only partly opens lock 3: a fifth of its bonds sit with foreigners, the ringgit is not a reserve currency, and reserves are about 0.9 times its short-term foreign debt. Malaysia's real brake on printing is the ringgit. If Bank Negara printed for the budget, foreign holders and savers could leave, and the ringgit would fall, raising the price of imports.
6. Game theory in five minutes
Game theory asks a simple question: what is each player's best move, given what the others might do? Six shapes of game explain a lot of what countries do.

rows: Everyone gains most if all act. Acting alone is costly
Fear decides whether all act or none
Each gains by cheating whatever the other does
So both cheat and both lose
A shared good is paid for by some and enjoyed by all
Each small player's best move is to let others pay
Many choices would work, so players pick the one everyone expects
The habit wins, even if others are as good
Two players drive at each other
Each tries to look more committed so the other swerves
Lenders who expect others to stay, stay. Those who expect others to flee, flee first
The same borrower can be safe or bust depending on belief

blocks.label: What game theory leaves out
blocks.text: Domestic politics (a leader facing an election may choose the worse national outcome), ideology, accidents and plain error. Use the games as a lens on incentives, not as proof that every move was planned.
7. Five questions that open the game board
Guess each answer before you open it. Each one opens a game, and each game is a real case.

items.q: Why did the G20 move within months in 2008 to 2009, but take years on poor countries' debts?
items.a: Two different games. In 2008 every member faced the same collapse, so acting together was each one's best move: $1.1 trillion and a $5 trillion spending push in one statement (coordination). Debt relief is a free-rider game: relief given by one lender frees cash to pay the others. The 2020 pause covered $12.9 billion, but only one private lender joined, and Ethiopia's deal took more than five years.

items.q: If every country wants a cheaper currency or a tariff edge, what happens when they all try at once?
items.a: A prisoner's dilemma: each gains alone, all lose together, as in the 1930s. In 2010 Brazil's finance minister said the world was in an international currency war. The exits have been deals like the 1985 Plaza Accord, or truces like the October 2025 US and China pause, which can lapse. When two giants face off with threats, it becomes chicken.

items.q: Why does the world keep saving in US dollars even while complaining about the US?
items.a: A focal point. Money is useful because others use it. The dollar was still 56.7% of world reserves in mid 2026, nearly three times the euro, while the Chinese yuan was 2.1% because China keeps capital controls. Switching only pays if many switch at once.

items.q: Why did Malaysia and its neighbours pile up dollars after 1998 instead of spending them?
items.a: Self-insurance. In 1997 to 1998 the ringgit fell from about 2.50 to about 4.88, and Thailand, Indonesia and Korea had to accept IMF conditions. Malaysia chose controls and a peg instead. Its reserves rose from $21.5 billion in 1997 to $132.6 billion in June 2026. Insurance you hold yourself is expensive, but nobody can attach conditions to it.

items.q: Why can Japan owe about twice its economy and borrow cheaply, while Sri Lanka defaulted, and where does Malaysia sit?
items.a: The run game: who holds the debt, and in which money, decides it. Japan owes yen mostly to itself, with its central bank holding about 41% and foreigners about 13%. Sri Lanka owed dollars to foreigners and stopped paying on 12 April 2022. Malaysia owes ringgit, 98.8% at home, but a fifth is held by foreigners, so its risk is a weaker ringgit, not default.

blocks.label: A sixth game: the race to the bottom on tax

blocks.text: Countries gain by undercutting each other's tax rates to attract company profits, and all lose revenue if all undercut. That is a prisoner's dilemma, and the 2021 deal set a 15% floor. Malaysia applied it from 1 January 2025. The US did not enact it, and in January 2026 the OECD package shielded US-based groups from the main top-up rules. The largest player took the defector's payoff, and the others accepted it to keep the rest of the deal. The US argues its own minimum taxes do a similar job, which is a real debate, not only defection.

blocks.label: Three balance-sheet walks: the dollar privilege, defending the ringgit, a euro member borrowing

blocks.text: The dollar privilege. A US household buys Malaysian-made chips. The exporter sells the dollars to its bank, which sells them to Bank Negara, which buys US Treasury bills. No dollars were created abroad. Dollars moved from a US household to a foreign central bank, which lent them back to the US government. The US got goods for IOUs in its own money. Bank Negara created ringgit to buy the dollars, and usually soaks them back up later.

Defending the ringgit. A foreign fund sells Malaysian bonds and wants dollars. Bank Negara sells dollars from its reserves and receives ringgit, so banks' ringgit reserves fall. It then usually tops them back up to keep its interest rate at 2.75%. The cost is dollar reserves, which is why the 0.9 times ratio matters. A defence that lasts too long runs reserves down, as in 1997 to 1998.

A euro member borrowing. Italy spends more than it taxes. It must sell bonds to banks, funds, households and foreigners. The ECB can create euros and buy Italian bonds on the resale market, but only by a decision taken for the whole euro area. In a panic, deposits can move to banks in another euro country, as in Greece, where about EUR 41 billion left before the June 2015 controls.
Say it back

blocks.q: A friend says any country can print its way out of debt. What three locks would you ask about?
blocks.a: Does it issue its own currency, does it owe its debt in that currency, and will markets let it print a lot without the currency crashing or inflation taking off?

blocks.q: Malaysia owes 98.8% of its federal debt at home, yet a sell-off by foreigners can still weaken the ringgit. Why, and which rung is it on?
blocks.a: Foreigners hold about a fifth of its government bonds and can leave the currency, so it only partly opens lock 3. Rung 3, near the top.

blocks.q: Which game explains why the world still saves in dollars?
blocks.a: A focal point. Money is useful because others use it, so switching pays only if many switch together.

Clubs deliver in crises and drift in calm years. Read every summit against the regime it meets in.

Malaysia's brake is the ringgit. Watch who holds its bonds, not only how much it owes.
In any headline about countries, ask which game is being played and who gains by moving first.
